name: CVRP X-n1001-k43
description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 131 from one depot to serve the 1000 customers of the CVRPLIB X-set instance X-n1001-k43. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

sources.locator: The Truck Dispatching Problem

CVRPLIB instance table: X-n1001-k43 (customers, vehicle capacity, best known solution, optimality column), the instance file and the set conventions (Euclidean distance rounded to the nearest integer, total distance as cost, number of routes free).
CVRPLIB update log (7 pages, read in full): dated entries naming who reported each improved best known solution of X-n1001-k43 and with which method.

Uchoa, Pecin, Pessoa, Poggi, Vidal and Subramanian (2017), New benchmark instances for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (Crossref: European Journal of Operational Research, March 2017): the X instance set, its generator and attributes; a benchmark paper, so not counted as evidence.

requirements.datasets: CVRPLIB X instance file X-n1001-k43.vrp (galgos.inf.puc-rio.br/cvrplib, download/instance/id)

execution.interface: solve(inst) -> list of routes; a route is a list of customer ids from 1 to n in visiting order (the depot is node 0 and is not listed; empty routes are ignored). inst is a dict with n (number of customers), capacity, coords (array of shape (n + 1, 2), row 0 is the depot), demand (integer array of length n + 1, demand[0] = 0) and name. Score: the total cost, minimized.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n10001-k1570
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 479 from one depot to serve the 10000 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n10001-k1570. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n1468-k151
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 726 from one depot to serve the 1467 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n1468-k151. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Dantzig and Ramser pose the capacitated vehicle routing problem the evaluator scores; the AILS-II and HGS-CVRP papers have solving large CVRP instances as their main objective and are the methods behind the initial and the later records of the XL set (per the XL paper's Table 1 and the CVRPLIB update log).
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a minimum-cost set of capacity-feasible vehicle routes from one depot that serves every customer of the CVRPLIB XL instance XL-n1701-k562, a large-scale instance with 1,000 to 10,000 customers.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Large-scale distribution routing with thousands of customers and routes of up to 200 stops is practical, and the XL instances were generated with the X-set scheme to cover its attributes, but they are beyond the reach of exact methods. In a 30-day community challenge from 12 January 2026 participating teams submitted 1,932 improved best known solutions, and the records kept moving afterwards, so a lower cost is a new best known solution of an open large-scale instance.

papers.title: The Truck Dispatching Problem
papers.task_relation: The task's objective is the capacitated vehicle routing cost (rounded Euclidean distances, free number of routes) on the fixed CVRPLIB instance XL-n1701-k562.
papers.primary_goal: Formulate and solve the routing of a fleet of capacitated trucks from a terminal to service stations, introducing the capacitated vehicle routing problem.

papers.title: AILS-II: An Adaptive Iterated Local Search Heuristic for the Large-Scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
papers.task_relation: Table 1 of the XL instance paper (arXiv:2601.11467) lists AILS-II as the method of the initial best known solution for 93 of the 100 XL instances, before the 2026 challenge improved them; the task asks for a cost below the current best known solution of XL-n1701-k562.
papers.primary_goal: Solve large-scale capacitated vehicle routing instances with an adaptive iterated local search heuristic.

papers.title: Hybrid genetic search for the CVRP: Open-source implementation and SWAP* neighborhood
papers.task_relation: The CVRPLIB update log credits many later XL records (Breunig, Seman, Bian) to runs that start from the published best known solution and re-solve subsets of routes with HGS-CVRP or a modified HGS; this paper presents the HGS-CVRP code, and it does not describe the XL records themselves.
papers.primary_goal: Present an open-source hybrid genetic search for the capacitated vehicle routing problem with the SWAP* neighbourhood and show that it improves the state of the art on CVRP benchmark instances.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n1701-k562
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 227 from one depot to serve the 1700 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n1701-k562. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

Score: the total cost, minimized.

science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Dantzig and Ramser pose the capacitated vehicle routing problem the evaluator scores; the AILS-II and HGS-CVRP papers have solving large CVRP instances as their main objective and are the methods behind the initial and the later records of the XL set (per the XL paper's Table 1 and the CVRPLIB update log).
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a minimum-cost set of capacity-feasible vehicle routes from one depot that serves every customer of the CVRPLIB XL instance XL-n2867-k120, a large-scale instance with 1,000 to 10,000 customers.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Large-scale distribution routing with thousands of customers and routes of up to 200 stops is practical, and the XL instances were generated with the X-set scheme to cover its attributes, but they are beyond the reach of exact methods. In a 30-day community challenge from 12 January 2026 participating teams submitted 1,932 improved best known solutions, and the records kept moving afterwards, so a lower cost is a new best known solution of an open large-scale instance.

papers.title: The Truck Dispatching Problem
papers.task_relation: The task's objective is the capacitated vehicle routing cost (rounded Euclidean distances, free number of routes) on the fixed CVRPLIB instance XL-n2867-k120.
papers.primary_goal: Formulate and solve the routing of a fleet of capacitated trucks from a terminal to service stations, introducing the capacitated vehicle routing problem.

papers.title: AILS-II: An Adaptive Iterated Local Search Heuristic for the Large-Scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
papers.task_relation: Table 1 of the XL instance paper (arXiv:2601.11467) lists AILS-II as the method of the initial best known solution for 93 of the 100 XL instances, before the 2026 challenge improved them; the task asks for a cost below the current best known solution of XL-n2867-k120.
papers.primary_goal: Solve large-scale capacitated vehicle routing instances with an adaptive iterated local search heuristic.

papers.title: Hybrid genetic search for the CVRP: Open-source implementation and SWAP* neighborhood
papers.task_relation: The CVRPLIB update log credits many later XL records (Breunig, Seman, Bian) to runs that start from the published best known solution and re-solve subsets of routes with HGS-CVRP or a modified HGS; this paper presents the HGS-CVRP code, and it does not describe the XL records themselves.
papers.primary_goal: Present an open-source hybrid genetic search for the capacitated vehicle routing problem with the SWAP* neighbourhood and show that it improves the state of the art on CVRP benchmark instances.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n2867-k120
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 180 from one depot to serve the 2866 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n2867-k120. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 20 from one depot to serve the 3333 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n3334-k934. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 598 from one depot to serve the 4062 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n4063-k347. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n4535-k1134
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 4 from one depot to serve the 4534 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n4535-k1134. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n5061-k184
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 206 from one depot to serve the 5060 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n5061-k184. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n7037-k38
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 187 from one depot to serve the 7036 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n7037-k38. Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a minimum-cost set of capacity-feasible vehicle routes from one depot that serves every customer of the CVRPLIB XL instance XL-n9784-k2774, a large-scale instance with 1,000 to 10,000 customers.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Large-scale distribution routing with thousands of customers and routes of up to 200 stops is practical, and the XL instances were generated with the X-set scheme to cover its attributes, but they are beyond the reach of exact methods. In a 30-day community challenge from 12 January 2026 participating teams submitted 1,932 improved best known solutions, and the records kept moving afterwards, so a lower cost is a new best known solution of an open large-scale instance.

papers.title: The Truck Dispatching Problem
papers.task_relation: The task's objective is the capacitated vehicle routing cost (rounded Euclidean distances, free number of routes) on the fixed CVRPLIB instance XL-n9784-k2774.
papers.primary_goal: Formulate and solve the routing of a fleet of capacitated trucks from a terminal to service stations, introducing the capacitated vehicle routing problem.

papers.title: AILS-II: An Adaptive Iterated Local Search Heuristic for the Large-Scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
papers.task_relation: Table 1 of the XL instance paper (arXiv:2601.11467) lists AILS-II as the method of the initial best known solution for 93 of the 100 XL instances, before the 2026 challenge improved them; the task asks for a cost below the current best known solution of XL-n9784-k2774.
papers.primary_goal: Solve large-scale capacitated vehicle routing instances with an adaptive iterated local search heuristic.

papers.title: Hybrid genetic search for the CVRP: Open-source implementation and SWAP* neighborhood
papers.task_relation: The CVRPLIB update log credits many later XL records (Breunig, Seman, Bian) to runs that start from the published best known solution and re-solve subsets of routes with HGS-CVRP or a modified HGS; this paper presents the HGS-CVRP code, and it does not describe the XL records themselves.
papers.primary_goal: Present an open-source hybrid genetic search for the capacitated vehicle routing problem with the SWAP* neighbourhood and show that it improves the state of the art on CVRP benchmark instances.

source_specification.name: CVRP XL-n9784-k2774
source_specification.description: Route identical vehicles of capacity 19 from one depot to serve the 9783 customers of the CVRPLIB XL-set instance XL-n9784-k2774. Every customer is visited exactly once, the total demand on a route may not exceed the capacity, and every route starts and ends at the depot. The number of routes is free (the k in the instance name does not limit it). Minimise the total cost: the sum over all routes of the Euclidean distances between consecutive stops, the legs from and to the depot included, each distance rounded to the nearest integer.

science_relevance.reason: The four papers have the size of DNA codes with constant GC-content and a minimum Hamming distance as their main objective and are the sources of the lower bounds in the Gaborit-King table that the task instance comes from; the evaluator checks exactly the code definition of King (2003).
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a DNA code of length 16 (words over A, C, G, T with exactly floor(16/2) letters from C and G, pairwise Hamming distance at least 12, and every word at distance at least 12 from the reverse complement of every word, itself included) with as many words as possible.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Requiring a word to be far from the reverse complement of every word, itself included, makes hybridisation of a word with any other word or with itself unlikely, which is the condition DNA tags and barcodes need; combined with constant GC-content it gives similar melting temperatures. The maximum size is unknown for almost all parameters and the pinned table has been the reference for lower bounds since 2010.

papers.title: Bounds for DNA Codes with Constant GC-Content
papers.task_relation: The paper defines the quantity the task maximises for length 16 and distance 12 (GC-content floor(16/2)); its lexicographic constructions and Johnson-type bounds underlie the table the task starts from. The task covers the reverse-complement variant (every word also at distance at least 12 from the reverse complement of every word, itself included).
papers.primary_goal: Derive upper and lower bounds on the maximum size of DNA codes with constant GC-content and minimum Hamming distance, with and without the reverse-complement constraint, and construct larger codes than previously published.

papers.title: Linear constructions for DNA codes
papers.task_relation: Its constructions give many entries of the table for length 16 and distance 12 (superscripts c, l and m on the pinned page); the task asks to beat the tabulated size. papers.primary_goal: Construct DNA codes with constant GC-content from linear and related codes and tabulate the resulting lower bounds.

source_specification.name: DNA code A4GC,RC(16,12)
source_specification.description: Find as many DNA words of length 16 as possible, that is, strings over the letters A, C, G, T, such that all words have the same number of letters in {C, G} (that number is free) and any two different words differ in at least 12 positions. In addition, the reverse complement of every word (the word read backwards with A and T exchanged and C and G exchanged) must differ in at least 12 positions from every word of the code, the word itself included.
source_specification.execution_notes: No data files.

Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: The four papers have the size of DNA codes with constant GC-content and a minimum Hamming distance as their main objective and are the sources of the lower bounds in the Gaborit-King table that the task instance comes from; the evaluator checks exactly the code definition of King (2003).
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a DNA code of length 17 (words over A, C, G, T with exactly floor(17/2) letters from C and G, pairwise Hamming distance at least 12, and every word at distance at least 12 from the reverse complement of every word, itself included) with as many words as possible.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Requiring a word to be far from the reverse complement of every word, itself included, makes hybridisation of a word with any other word or with itself unlikely, which is the condition DNA tags and barcodes need; combined with constant GC-content it gives similar melting temperatures. The maximum size is unknown for almost all parameters and the pinned table has been the reference for lower bounds since 2010.

papers.title: Bounds for DNA Codes with Constant GC-Content
papers.task_relation: The paper defines the quantity the task maximises for length 17 and distance 12 (GC-content floor(17/2)); its lexicographic constructions and Johnson-type bounds underlie the table the task starts from. The task covers the reverse-complement variant (every word also at distance at least 12 from the reverse complement of every word, itself included).
papers.primary_goal: Derive upper and lower bounds on the maximum size of DNA codes with constant GC-content and minimum Hamming distance, with and without the reverse-complement constraint, and construct larger codes than previously published.

papers.title: Linear constructions for DNA codes
papers.task_relation: Its constructions give many entries of the table for length 17 and distance 12 (superscripts c, l and m on the pinned page); the task asks to beat the tabulated size. Covers the reverse-complement variant (every word also at distance at least 12 from the reverse complement of every word, itself included).
papers.primary_goal: Construct DNA codes with constant GC-content from linear and related codes and tabulate the resulting lower bounds.

papers.title: Improved Lower Bounds for Constant GC-Content DNA Codes
papers.task_relation: Supplies table entries marked a, b and colon-optimal on the pinned page; the task asks for a larger code than the tabulated one for length 17, distance 12.
papers.primary_goal: Improve the lower bounds on the size of constant GC-content DNA codes, with and without the reverse-complement constraint, by stochastic local search, and prove some entries optimal by clique computations.

papers.title: Construction of Constant GC-Content DNA Codes via a Variable Neighbourhood Search Algorithm
papers.task_relation: Supplies the many table entries marked v on the pinned page; the task asks for a larger code for length 17, distance 12.
papers.primary_goal: Construct large constant GC-content DNA codes with a variable neighbourhood search algorithm.

source_specification.name: DNA code A4GC,RC(17,12)
source_specification.description: Find as many DNA words of length 17 as possible, that is, strings over the letters A, C, G, T, such that all words have the same number of letters in {C, G} (that number is free) and any two different words differ in at least 12 positions. In addition, the reverse complement of every word (the word read backwards with A and T exchanged and C and G exchanged) must differ in at least 12 positions from every word of the code, the word itself included.
source_specification.execution_notes: No data files.

execution.interface: construct() -> list of distinct strings of length 20 over the capital letters A, C, G, T (at least one word and at most 20000; a longer list is invalid). Score: number of words, maximized.
notes: No data files.

limitations: The record is the proven maximum: by the Plotkin bound a code over {A, C, G, T} of length 20 and distance 16 has at most 16 words, and a reverse-complement code C gives the code C together with the reverse complements of its words, of twice its size, so nothing can beat it; a result can only match it.

The record is the lower bound of Aboluion, Smith and Perkins, Discrete Mathematics 312 (2012), marked there as a new best known result (also the 2011 PhD thesis of Aboluion). The codeword file of the archive named in the paper is replayed word by word through this task's verifier. The codes of these authors have only even GC weights, so for some cells the weight is not floor(n/2); the task lets the code choose its weight. The values are algebraic constructions (cyclic additive codes, cosets, shortening): a plain search reaches 62 to 85% of them (REVIEW.md, section 21). The tables of Montemanni, Smith and Koul (2014) show no larger value.
Only open entries with a bound of at most 2000 words in the table are tasks, so that the pairwise check stays cheap.

The paper Zenodo archive was downloaded, its published MD5 verified, and source inspected. It provides the exact run_BP_HPO.py script and frozen library; see archive_execution. Commands run in the extracted paper archive; the current GitHub checkout is a separate, later implementation.

Archived BP raw evaluator returns (mean bins used - mean L1 lower bound) / mean L1 lower bound: a dimensionless excess fraction to minimize, with no multiplication by 100. run_BP_HPO.py negates this value for maximization.
Paper Section4.1 instead defines mean_i(lb_i / n_i), a ratio to maximize. This differs from the archived score in formula and scale; both definitions are preserved separately.

name: EPFL adder, LUT-6 levels
description: Optimise the EPFL combinational benchmark circuit adder (adds two 128-bit numbers; 256 inputs, 129 outputs) with the logic-synthesis tool ABC and map it to lookup tables (LUTs) with at most 6 inputs, minimising the number of LUT levels, the largest number of LUTs on a path from an input to an output. The result must compute the same function as the original circuit.

sources.locator: adder
FlowMap: an optimal technology mapping algorithm for delay optimization in lookup-table based FPGA designs
Circuit Minimization with QBF-Based Exact Synthesis
EPFL benchmark repository: adder circuit files and best_results/README.md (best LUT-6 counts and levels, 2026).

Amaru, Gaillardon and De Micheli (2015), The EPFL Combinational Benchmark Suite (title read in the PDF text): circuit descriptions and input/output counts for adder; a benchmark paper, so not primary evidence.

execution.interface: script() -> string of ABC commands separated by `;` or newlines. The evaluator runs `read <circuit>; <script>` in ABC and writes out the network the script leaves. That network must consist only of LUTs with at most 6 inputs (in ABC a LUT mapper such as `if -K 6` produces one; library gates or a wider node are invalid), and it must be equivalent to the original circuit, which a separate ABC process checks with `cec`. The script may not contain the characters ! / \ ~, may not use commands that read or write files, change the session or start other programs (read*, write*, load*, dump*, save* and their short forms, source, alias, set, unset, history, cd, ls, pwd, quit, exit), and may not ask for LUTs wider than 6 inputs (-K above 6). Time limits: 1200 s for the script, 900 s for the equivalence check. A script that is refused, fails, runs out of time or changes the function is invalid. Score: the largest number of LUTs with two or more inputs on a path from an input to an output (buffers, inverters and constants are not counted), minimized.
notes: arithmetic/adder.aig from github.com/lsils/benchmarks

limitations: Most records come from SAT-based exact synthesis of subcircuits, which an ABC script cannot express.
Requires the Berkeley ABC binary (set ARNEW_ABC).
LUTs and levels are counted from the written network by the convention of the EPFL table (single-input nodes are free), not from ABC's print_stats.

papers.task_relation: Tyrrell constructs larger cap sets to improve mathematical lower bounds. This task searches F₃⁸ using a greedy priority rule; the finite dimension and search mechanism are local restrictions of the same cap-set construction objective.

name: Max-cut, G-set G1
description: Partition the 800 vertices of the G-set graph G1 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). The graph is undirected and has 19176 edges, each given once; every edge has weight 1.

sources.locator: G1
2025 report of G81 14060 and related cuts
An Application of Combinatorial Optimization to Statistical Physics and Circuit Layout Design
Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability problems using semidefinite programming
Rank-Two Relaxation Heuristics for MAX-CUT and Other Binary Quadratic Programs
Breakout Local Search for the Max-Cutproblem

Helmberg and Rendl (2000), A Spectral Bundle Method for Semidefinite Programming (title per Crossref): a semidefinite programming method, not a max-cut paper; the brief credits it with the first use of the G-set, which was not checked.

Khan and Shukla (2025), New Best-Known Max-Cut Solution for the G63 Instance in the G-Set Benchmark: describes the set as random, toroidal and planar graphs with 1 or +-1 weights, and gives the earlier best value for G63.

execution.interface: solve(n, edges) -> sequence of n integers, each 0 or 1: the side of every vertex. edges is an int64 array with one row (i, j, w) per edge, vertices numbered from 0. Score: total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides, maximized.
notes: G-set file G1 from https://web.stanford.edu/~yyye/yyye/Gset/G1

limitations: Specialised solvers (breakout local search, simulated bifurcation, GES-PR) are strong on this set.
The data file digest is not pinned until scripts/prepare_new_data.py has fetched it.
The task states no record. See VALIDITY.md.

science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: The cited papers have the max-cut problem (its applications, its semidefinite relaxation and heuristics for large instances) as their main objective, and the evaluator scores exactly the cut weight on a pinned G-set graph.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G1 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. It is equivalent to finding a ground state of an Ising spin glass without external field, and it models via minimisation in circuit layout; its semidefinite relaxation gave one of the best-known approximation algorithms. The G-set graphs (800 to 20,000 vertices) have been a standard test bed for heuristics and Ising machines for about 25 years, and for the large sparse graphs a better cut is a better solution of an open or unproven instance.

papers.title: An Application of Combinatorial Optimization to Statistical Physics and Circuit Layout Design
papers.task_relation: States why max-cut matters (spin-glass ground states, layout); the task scores the max-cut weight of the G-set graph G1, with a heuristic instead of a cutting-plane method.
papers.primary_goal: Reduce spin-glass ground states and via minimisation in circuit layout to max-cut and solve the resulting instances with a cutting-plane algorithm.

papers.title: Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability problems using semidefinite programming
papers.task_relation: Introduces the semidefinite relaxation that bounds and approximates the quantity the task maximises; the task has no guarantee requirement.
papers.primary_goal: Give a randomised approximation algorithm for max-cut based on a semidefinite programming relaxation.

papers.title: Rank-Two Relaxation Heuristics for MAX-CUT and Other Binary Quadratic Programs
papers.task_relation: A heuristic for large max-cut graphs of the kind the task poses; the task asks for a better cut on one fixed graph. The paper's use of the G-set files was not read.
papers.primary_goal: Develop fast rank-two relaxation heuristics for large max-cut instances and compare them with semidefinite programming codes.

papers.title: Breakout Local Search for the Max-Cutproblem
papers.task_relation: A heuristic whose main objective is the cut weight the task scores on G-set graphs. The title is as Crossref spells it; its tables were not read (publisher page blocked).
papers.primary_goal: Design a breakout local search heuristic for max-cut and report improved cuts on benchmark graphs.

source_specification.name: Max-cut, G-set G12
source_specification.description: Partition the 800 vertices of the G-set graph G12 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G13 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G19 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).

source_specification.name: Max-cut, G-set G29
source_specification.description: Partition the 2000 vertices of the G-set graph G29 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). name: Max-cut, G-set G3

The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. science_relevance.reason: The cited papers have the max-cut problem (its applications, its semidefinite relaxation and heuristics for large instances) as their main objective, and the evaluator scores exactly the cut weight on a pinned G-set graph.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G3 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. It is equivalent to finding a ground state of an Ising spin glass without external field, and it models via minimisation in circuit layout; its semidefinite relaxation gave one of the best-known approximation algorithms. The G-set graphs (800 to 20,000 vertices) have been a standard test bed for heuristics and Ising machines for about 25 years, and for the large sparse graphs a better cut is a better solution of an open or unproven instance.

papers.primary_goal: Reduce spin-glass ground states and via minimisation in circuit layout to max-cut and solve the resulting instances with a cutting-plane algorithm.

source_specification.name: Max-cut, G-set G34
source_specification.description: Partition the 2000 vertices of the G-set graph G34 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). The graph is undirected and has 4000 edges, each given once; every edge has weight 1 or -1, and an edge of weight -1 that is cut lowers the total.

The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: The cited papers have the max-cut problem (its applications, its semidefinite relaxation and heuristics for large instances) as their main objective, and the evaluator scores exactly the cut weight on a pinned G-set graph.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G35 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. It is equivalent to finding a ground state of an Ising spin glass without external field, and it models via minimisation in circuit layout; its semidefinite relaxation gave one of the best-known approximation algorithms. The G-set graphs (800 to 20,000 vertices) have been a standard test bed for heuristics and Ising machines for about 25 years, and for the large sparse graphs a better cut is a better solution of an open or unproven instance.

papers.primary_goal: Reduce spin-glass ground states and via minimisation in circuit layout to max-cut and solve the resulting instances with a cutting-plane algorithm.

source_specification.execution_notes: G-set file G4 from https://web.stanford.edu/~yyye/yyye/Gset/G4

name: Max-cut, G-set G40
description: Partition the 2000 vertices of the G-set graph G40 into two sides so that the total weight of the edges whose endpoints are on different sides is as large as possible (max-cut). The graph is undirected and has 11766 edges, each given once; every edge has weight 1 or -1, and an edge of weight -1 that is cut lowers the total.

sources.locator: 2025 report of G81 14060 and related cuts

notes: G-set file G40 from https://web.stanford.edu/~yyye/yyye/Gset/G40

limitations: Specialised solvers (breakout local search, simulated bifurcation, GES-PR) are strong on this set.

science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. The evidence must explain why the problem matters and how the local task represents it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: The cited papers have the max-cut problem (its applications, its semidefinite relaxation and heuristics for large instances) as their main objective, and the evaluator scores exactly the cut weight on a pinned G-set graph.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G40 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. It is equivalent to finding a ground state of an Ising spin glass without external field, and it models via minimisation in circuit layout; its semidefinite relaxation gave one of the best-known approximation algorithms. The G-set graphs (800 to 20,000 vertices) have been a standard test bed for heuristics and Ising machines for about 25 years, and for the large sparse graphs a better cut is a better solution of an open or unproven instance.

papers.title: An Application of Combinatorial Optimization to Statistical Physics and Circuit Layout Design
papers.task_relation: States why max-cut matters (spin-glass ground states, layout); the task scores the max-cut weight of the G-set graph G40, with a heuristic instead of a cutting-plane method.
papers.primary_goal: Reduce spin-glass ground states and via minimisation in circuit layout to max-cut and solve the resulting instances with a cutting-plane algorithm.

papers.title: Improved approximation algorithms for maximum cut and satisfiability problems using semidefinite programming
papers.task_relation: Introduces the semidefinite relaxation that bounds and approximates the quantity the task maximises; the task has no guarantee requirement.

science_relevance.reason: The cited papers have the max-cut problem (its applications, its semidefinite relaxation and heuristics for large instances) as their main objective, and the evaluator scores exactly the cut weight on a pinned G-set graph.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a partition of the vertices of the G-set graph G9 into two sides that maximises the total weight of the edges between the sides (max-cut).
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Max-cut asks for the heaviest cut of a weighted graph and is NP-hard. It is equivalent to finding a ground state of an Ising spin glass without external field, and it models via minimisation in circuit layout; its semidefinite relaxation gave one of the best-known approximation algorithms. The G-set graphs (800 to 20,000 vertices) have been a standard test bed for heuristics and Ising machines for about 25 years, and for the large sparse graphs a better cut is a better solution of an open or unproven instance.

papers.primary_goal: Develop fast rank-two relaxation heuristics for large max-cut instances and compare them with semidefinite programming codes.

name: Job-shop scheduling dmu11
description: Schedule 30 jobs on 15 machines (job-shop benchmark instance dmu11). Every job is a sequence of 15 operations, one on each machine, that must run in the given order; an operation occupies its machine for its whole duration without interruption, and a machine processes one operation at a time. Minimise the makespan, the time at which the last operation ends.

source_specification.name: Job-shop scheduling dmu12
source_specification.description: Schedule 30 jobs on 15 machines (job-shop benchmark instance dmu12). Every job is a sequence of 15 operations, one on each machine, that must run in the given order; an operation occupies its machine for its whole duration without interruption, and a machine processes one operation at a time. name: Santa 2025: Christmas tree packing (n = 1..200)
description: For every n from 1 to 200 place n copies of the competition's fixed 15-vertex tree polygon (rotations allowed, no overlaps, coordinates within [-100, 100]) so that the bounding square of each configuration is as small as possible; the score is the sum over n of (bounding-square area / n), lower is better.

sources.locator: Competition overview and evaluation page (task statement, metric definition, submission format)
Getting-started notebook (tree geometry, collision rule, greedy sample submission)
santa-2025-metric.py (official metric, shapely 2.1.2), sample_submission.csv

evaluation.benchmark: Kaggle Santa 2025 - Christmas Tree Packing Challenge
evaluation.paper_metric: sum over n of bounding-square area / n

execution.interface: construct(n) -> array of shape (n, 3): rows (x, y, deg) for the n-tree configuration; called for every n in 1..200

limitations: The evaluator is an independent reimplementation of the competition metric (same polygon, scaling factor, overlap rule and bounding-square formula) and reproduces the official code's doctest value and the sample submission's score exactly; it is not the Kaggle scoring service.
No leaderboard value is embedded; the reference value is the getting-started sample submission (176.60550959158516).

notes: Default direct-evaluation profile: official IOH BBOB function 10, dimension5, held-out instance4, exactly100 calls, one run, seed0.

Full paper evaluation: dimensions5/10/20/40, held-out instances4/5/6, budget10*d+50, five repetitions. Original broader commands are retained separately; the default adapter does not reproduce that complete experiment.
The released primary `.score` uses normalized trapezoidal area over log10 best-objective gaps clipped to [1e-8,1e4] at d5 (upper1e9 above d5). The separate IOH logger metric is not substituted.

Original class interface preserved: Optimizer(dim,budget)(func) returns(best_y,best_x). A new small GP/EI baseline keeps evaluation CPU-cheap. Strict complete-budget/finite/domain checks are added by this repository harness.

limitations: Execution interface inspected in pinned source. Full paper experiments have not been reproduced here.

setup_instructions.notes: Minimal dependency subset for this adapter; avoids optional provider, Botorch, embedding and plotting frameworks.

task_setup_instructions.notes: Minimal dependency subset for this adapter; avoids optional provider, Botorch, embedding and plotting frameworks.

notes: Default direct-evaluation profile: official IOH BBOB function 17, dimension5, held-out instance4, exactly100 calls, one run, seed0.

Full paper evaluation: dimensions5/10/20/40, held-out instances4/5/6, budget10*d+50, five repetitions. Original broader commands are retained separately; the default adapter does not reproduce that complete experiment.
The released primary `.score` uses normalized trapezoidal area over log10 best-objective gaps clipped to [1e-8,1e4] at d5 (upper1e9 above d5). The separate IOH logger metric is not substituted.

Original class interface preserved: Optimizer(dim,budget)(func) returns(best_y,best_x). A new small GP/EI baseline keeps evaluation CPU-cheap. Strict complete-budget/finite/domain checks are added by this repository harness.

limitations: Execution interface inspected in pinned source. Full paper experiments have not been reproduced here.

name: Quadratic assignment, QAPLIB sko100a
description: Quadratic assignment problem, QAPLIB instance sko100a: given two 100 x 100 integer matrices a and b, find a permutation p of 0..99 that minimises the cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]]. In the usual reading one matrix holds the flows between facilities and the other the distances between locations, and p assigns the one to the other; the cost formula is what is scored.

sources.locator: sko100a
QAPLIB, table of instances and solutions: sko100a (best known value and lower bound)
Assignment Problems and the Location of Economic Activities
Tabu Search Applied to the Quadratic Assignment Problem
Genetic hybrids for the quadratic assignment problem
QAPLIB instance descriptions (sections Skorin-Kapov, Taillard, Thonemann and Boelte, Wilhelm and Ward), best known values with their method codes, and lower bounds.
Burkard, Karisch and Rendl (1997), QAPLIB - a quadratic assignment problem library: instance definitions and conventions (library paper, not evidence).

requirements.datasets: sko100a.dat from the QAPLIB deposit (Edinburgh DataShare, doi 10.7488/ds/3428, CC BY 4.0)

execution.interface: solve(a, b) -> permutation p of 0..n-1 (a list of n integers, each exactly once). a and b are the first and second matrix of the QAPLIB file (int64 arrays of shape (n, n), passed as copies). Score: the exact integer cost, the sum over all i and j of a[i, j] * b[p[i], p[j]], minimized.
notes: sko100a.dat from the QAPLIB deposit (Edinburgh DataShare, doi 10.7488/ds/3428, CC BY 4.0)

science_relevance.definition: A task is important to science when it addresses a substantive scientific or real-world problem, and a cited research paper's main objective is to solve that problem or advance understanding of it. Using a task to evaluate an agent, framework, or general-purpose model, or citing only a benchmark, dataset, or tool, does not establish scientific importance.
science_relevance.reason: Each cited paper has the quadratic assignment problem, or the search for good QAPLIB solutions, as its main objective; the evaluator scores exactly the QAP cost of a permutation on the pinned instance.
science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find a minimum-cost Koopmans-Beckmann quadratic assignment of 100 facilities to 100 locations for the QAPLIB instance sko100a, which is not solved to optimality.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: The quadratic assignment problem models facility and hospital layout, keyboard design, backboard wiring and the generation of grey patterns. It is NP-hard and hard in practice: QAPLIB instances above about 30 facilities are mostly unsolved, and the best known solutions of the larger ones have stood for many years, so a cheaper permutation is a new best known solution of a standard open instance.

papers.title: Assignment Problems and the Location of Economic Activities
papers.task_relation: The task's objective is the Koopmans-Beckmann quadratic assignment cost of the QAPLIB instance sko100a.
papers.primary_goal: Formulate the assignment of indivisible economic activities to locations, introducing the quadratic assignment problem.

papers.title: Tabu Search Applied to the Quadratic Assignment Problem
papers.task_relation: QAPLIB credits the Skorin-Kapov instance set (rectangular-grid distances, pseudorandom flows) to this paper, and lists strict tabu search from it as a heuristic; sko100a belongs to that set.
papers.primary_goal: Apply tabu search to the quadratic assignment problem.

papers.title: Genetic hybrids for the quadratic assignment problem
papers.task_relation: QAPLIB credits the best known solution of sko100a to this genetic hybrid (GEN); the task asks to improve it.
papers.primary_goal: Design genetic algorithms hybridised with local search that find better solutions of QAPLIB instances.

transform_grid_attempt_1.docstring:
Example transformation:
- Validate input (2D, integer values 0-9).
- Rotate the grid 90 degrees clockwise.
- Increment every cell by 1 modulo 10 (keeps values 0-9).
Returns a new numpy int array.

transform_grid_attempt_2.docstring:
Example transformation:
- Validate input (2D, integer values 0-9).
- Upsample each cell to a 2x2 block (doubling both dimensions).
- Invert colors by mapping v -> 9 - v (keeps values 0-9).
Returns a new numpy int array.

arithmetic_kakeya_distribution.docstring:
Arithmetic Kakeya conjecture (entropy formulation). Construct a joint probability
distribution P[y, x] of two discrete random variables X, Y supported on an n x n grid
(here n = 10) so as to maximize the entropy projection ratio

    H(pi_{r_inf}) / max_i H(pi_{r_i}),

where pi_r(x, y) = x + r * y projects the grid along slope r, H is the Shannon entropy
(in bits) of the resulting projected distribution, the finite slopes are
r_1, ..., r_k = 0.0, 1.0, 2.0 and the distinguished slope is r_inf = -1.0.

The baseline is the uniform distribution over the grid.

Returns:
    P: np.ndarray of shape (10, 10), non-negative and summing to 1, where P[y, x] is the
        joint probability that X = x and Y = y.

block_stacking30.docstring:
Block-stacking (single-wide overhang) problem. Stack n identical rigid blocks of
width 1 at the edge of a table (table edge at x = 0). Let x_k be the horizontal
position of block k (its center), with 0 = x_0 <= x_1 <= ... <= x_n. Maximize the
horizontal displacement x_n of the top (n-th) block over the table edge subject to
the stack remaining stable, i.e. for every 0 <= i < n the center of mass of all
blocks above block i must lie within block i's footprint (and the whole stack's
center of mass must lie over the table). Here n = 30.

Baseline construction: the classical harmonic ("1/2, 1/4, 1/6, ...") staircase,
which achieves the known optimum C(n) = (1/2) * H_n, where H_n is the n-th harmonic
number. Block k is offset so that x_k = (1/2)(H_n - H_{n-k-1}).

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (30,) with the horizontal center positions
        x_1, ..., x_n of the blocks, non-decreasing and positive.

hausdorff_young_p32.docstring:
Hausdorff-Young inequality, probing the Babenko-Beckner constant.

Construct a bounded, integrable, not-identically-zero step function f of one real
variable that maximizes the quotient

    Q(f) = ||fhat||_q / ||f||_p ,     with 1/p + 1/q = 1, p = 3/2, q = 3,

where fhat is the Fourier transform fhat(xi) = integral f(x) exp(-2*pi*i*x*xi) dx.

The function is represented as a step function on the interval [-R, R]: cell j
(j = 0 .. N-1) spans [x_j, x_j + dx) with x_j = -R + j*dx and dx = 2R/N, and f takes
the constant value returned in entry j of the array. The sharp maximizer of the
Hausdorff-Young ratio is a Gaussian (Babenko-Beckner), so the baseline samples the
Gaussian exp(-x^2) on the grid.

Returns:
    values: np.ndarray of shape (N,), the step-function value of f on each grid cell.

crouzeix_conjecture4.docstring:
Crouzeix's conjecture probe. Find a complex n x n matrix A and a polynomial p
(given by its complex coefficients, highest degree first, as in numpy.poly1d)
that make the Crouzeix ratio

    R(A, p) = || p(A) ||_op  /  sup_{z in W(A)} |p(z)|

as large as possible, where || . ||_op is the spectral (operator) norm and

    W(A) = { <A x, x> : ||x|| <= 1 }

is the numerical range (field of values) of A. Crouzeix's conjecture states
that R(A, p) <= 2 for every A and p; the bound 2 is approached by the
construction below. Here the size is baked to n = 4.

The baseline is the AlphaEvolve "optimal" tridiagonal construction: a
nilpotent matrix with sqrt(2) on the first and last super-diagonal entries
and 1 on the interior super-diagonal entries, paired with p(z) = z^(n-1).

Returns:
    A: np.ndarray of shape (4, 4), complex dtype, the matrix.
    poly_coeffs: np.ndarray of shape (4,), the polynomial coefficients in
        descending-degree order (numpy.poly1d convention). Here this encodes
        p(z) = z^3.

equidistant_points_polygon20.docstring:
Build a convex polygon with n = 20 vertices that tries to be a counterexample to the
conjecture "every convex polygon has a vertex v with no 4 other vertices equidistant
from v". The goal is a polygon where EVERY vertex has (at least) 4 other vertices that
are approximately equidistant from it. Quality is the minimum, over all vertices, of a
per-vertex equidistance score in [0, 1] (1.0 = perfect counterexample).

This baseline is the upstream search's starting construction: a regular polygon whose
vertices lie evenly on a circle (deterministic, strictly convex). The scoring function
is scale/translation invariant, so the circle radius is arbitrary.

Returns:
    polygon: np.ndarray of shape (20, 2) with the x,y coordinates of the vertices,
        given in convex (counter-clockwise) order.

erdos_discrepancy_pattern.docstring:
Erdos discrepancy problem. Build the longest possible sign pattern
a_1, ..., a_N in {-1, +1} whose discrepancy is at most 2, where the
discrepancy is the maximum value of |a_d + a_{2d} + ... + a_{kd}| taken over
all homogeneous progressions d, 2d, ..., kd contained in {1, ..., N}.

This baseline uses a deterministic greedy construction: it appends signs one
at a time, at each step choosing the sign (+1 or -1) that keeps every
homogeneous-progression partial sum within [-2, 2], breaking ties by
minimizing the sum of squared partial sums. It stops as soon as neither sign
can be appended without exceeding discrepancy 2.

Returns:
    pattern: np.ndarray of shape (N,) and integer dtype, with every entry
        equal to +1 or -1. N is determined by how far the greedy
        construction can extend while keeping discrepancy <= 2.

erdos_gyarfas_graph.docstring:
Erdős-Gyárfás counterexample search. Construct a finite simple graph G whose
minimum degree is at least 3, trying to AVOID any cycle whose length is a power
of two (4, 8, 16, ...). The Erdős-Gyárfás conjecture states no such graph exists;
we search for a counterexample (or, failing that, a graph with as few power-of-two
cycles as possible).

The graph is represented by its adjacency matrix: a symmetric numpy array A of
shape (n, n) with entries in {0, 1} and zero diagonal, where A[i, j] = 1 iff there
is an edge between vertices i and j.

Baseline construction (translated from the notebook's nx.random_regular_graph(3, n)):
a random 3-regular graph on n vertices built with the configuration / pairing model,
deterministically seeded for reproducibility.

Returns:
    adjacency: np.ndarray of shape (n, n), symmetric, {0, 1}-valued, zero diagonal.

erdos_squarefree500.docstring:
Erdos squarefree problem. For N = 500, find a subset A of {1, ..., N} of maximum
size such that a*b + 1 is NOT square-free for every pair a, b in A (a square-free
integer is one not divisible by any perfect square > 1). Larger feasible subsets
are better; pairs whose a*b + 1 is square-free are penalized as violations.

Baseline construction: the residue class 7 (mod 25). If a, b == 7 (mod 25) then
a*b == 49 == -1 (mod 25), so a*b + 1 == 0 (mod 25) is divisible by 5^2 and is never
square-free. This yields zero violations for any pair drawn from the class.

Returns:
    subset: 1-D np.ndarray of distinct integers in {1, ..., 500} forming the subset A.

factoring_factorials100.docstring:
Factoring N! into N factors (here N = 100). Let A034258-style C(N) be the largest
quantity such that N! can be written as a product of exactly N integer factors that are
all >= C(N). Equivalently, partition the multiset of prime factors of N! into N groups
(bins) and maximize the minimum group product. The objective is to make the smallest of
the N factors as large as possible.

Solution representation (numpy-array form required by this template):
    The prime factors of N! are enumerated in a fixed canonical order: the sorted-ascending
    list of all prime factors of N! counted with multiplicity, e.g. [2, 2, ..., 3, 3, ...,
    5, ...]. This constructor returns a 1-D integer assignment array `assign` of that same
    length, where assign[i] in {0, ..., N-1} is the bin (factor) that the i-th canonical
    prime factor is placed into. The N factor values are then the products of the primes in
    each bin, and the score is the minimum of those N products.

Baseline construction:
    A multiplicative longest-processing-time greedy: sort the prime factors descending and
    repeatedly assign the next largest prime to the bin that currently has the smallest
    product (balancing the bins). Deterministic.

Returns:
    assign: np.ndarray of shape (Omega(N!),) and integer dtype, with values in [0, N-1],
        giving the bin index of each canonical prime factor. For N = 100 the length is 239.

kakeya_set.docstring:
Construct a Kakeya set in the finite plane F_p^2 with p = 7. A Kakeya set must
contain a full line in every direction. There are p + 1 = 8 directions: the p = 7
directions of slope m = 0, 1, ..., 6 (non-vertical lines y = m*x + b), and the 1
vertical direction (lines x = c). For each direction we choose the intercept. The
returned array of length 8 encodes those choices: entries[m] = b for the line of
slope m (m = 0..6), and entries[7] = c for the vertical line. The Kakeya set is the
union of these 8 chosen lines; the objective is to minimize the number of points in
the union.

Returns:
    entries: np.ndarray of shape (8,) integer intercepts (entries in [0,7)).

nikodym_set.docstring:
Construct a Nikodym set in F_q^2 with q = p^2 and p = 7. A set N is a Nikodym
set if, for every point x in F_q^2, there exists a direction v != 0 such that
the punctured line {x + t*v : t in F_q, t != 0} is fully contained in N. The
goal is to make N as SMALL as possible, equivalently to make its complement
(the excluded set) as LARGE as possible.

Field model: F_q is built as F_p[alpha] with alpha^2 = k, where k is the
smallest quadratic non-residue mod p. An element of F_q is the pair (a, b)
standing for a + b*alpha, with a, b in {0, ..., p-1}.

Baseline construction (the "skip step 2.5" construction from the AlphaEvolve
notebook, of size p^4 - p^2*(p+1)/2): take the Hermitian unital
    U = {(x, y) : Trace(x) + Norm(y) = 0},  with Trace((a,b)) = 2a,
    Norm((a,b)) = a^2 - b^2*k.
Build the blocking set B = points of U whose y-coordinate lies in the special
set Y = {(u^2 mod p, v) : u, v in F_p}. The excluded set is S = U \ B, and the
Nikodym set is everything else: N = (F_q^2) \ S.

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (k, 2, 2) integer array. Each of the k points
    is [[x_a, x_b], [y_a, y_b]] with the F_q coordinates x = (x_a, x_b) and
    y = (y_a, y_b), all entries in [0, p).

sum_product_set.docstring:
Construct a subset A of the finite field F_31 (integers mod 31) that minimizes
|A+A| + |A*A|, where A+A = { (a+b) mod 31 : a,b in A } and
A*A = { (a*b) mod 31 : a,b in A }. The sum-product phenomenon guarantees that at
least one of these sets must be large, so minimizing their combined size is a
genuine optimization. Here A has 12 distinct elements.

Returns:
    elements: np.ndarray of shape (12,) with distinct integer elements in [0, 31).

flat_polynomial.docstring:
Construct a binary sequence a of length N = 41 with entries in {-1, +1} that maximizes the

unit circle (low autocorrelation binary sequence).

function_guessing_game_strategy.docstring:
Offline proxy for AlphaEvolve Problem 66 ("The function guessing game").

In the original (interactive) problem, an agent must guess a hidden function
f: R -> R, paying 1 currency unit per evaluation f(x), and earning a reward of
1000 currency units if it reconstructs the function accurately (L^1 error below a
small threshold). The deterministic, offline core of that game is: decide AT WHICH
POINTS to evaluate the hidden function so that, given only those samples, the
function can be reconstructed exactly while paying as little as possible.

A guessing strategy is therefore a fixed set of query locations x_1, ..., x_k in the
domain [-1, 1]. The evaluator probes each hidden test function at these locations,
reconstructs it by polynomial (least-squares) interpolation, and scores the strategy
by the net reward = 1000 * (fraction reconstructed correctly) - k, i.e. reward minus
the per-evaluation query cost.

A polynomial of degree D is uniquely determined by D + 1 distinct samples, so the
optimal strategy queries exactly D + 1 well-placed points. This baseline plays it
safe with 12 equally-spaced query points: it reconstructs every degree-5 test
function exactly, but overpays on queries, leaving headroom for evolution to reduce
the number of queries toward the optimum of 6.

Returns:
    query_points: np.ndarray of shape (k,) giving the x-locations (in [-1, 1]) at
        which the hidden function will be evaluated.

furstenberg_sarkozy_205.docstring:
Furstenberg-Sarkozy problem (modular formulation). Find a subset of Z/mZ of maximum
size that does NOT contain any two elements differing by a nonzero perfect k-th power
modulo m. Here m = 205 and k = 2 (squares), i.e. forbidden differences are the nonzero
quadratic residues modulo 205.

The returned subset is the AlphaEvolve search target: the larger it is (while staying
feasible) the better. The AlphaEvolve record for this instance is a subset of size 12.

The notebook's literal search seed is the trivial subset [0]; here we use a slightly
stronger but still simple deterministic greedy construction as the starting point so
evolution has something concrete to improve on.

Returns:
    subset: np.ndarray of shape (s,), dtype int, a list of distinct residues in
        {0, ..., 204} with no two differing by a nonzero square modulo 205.

grid_tiling_imo2025_p6_n36.docstring:
IMO 2025 Problem 6 (grid tiling). On an n x n grid of unit squares, place
non-overlapping axis-aligned rectangular tiles (sides on grid lines) so that
every row and every column has exactly one uncovered unit square. Minimize the
number of tiles. Here n = 36 (optimal tile count is n + 2*sqrt(n) - 3 = 45).

Baseline construction: leave the main diagonal uncovered (one uncovered cell
per row and per column), then greedily cover the rest with maximal rectangles

plenty of room to improve toward the optimum.

kakeya_needle_2d_positions64.docstring:
Two-dimensional Kakeya-needle area-minimization problem. For a fixed n, choose
base positions x = (x_0, ..., x_{n-1}). For position index i (0-based) let
a_i = (i + 1) / n and define the triangle R_i with vertices
    (x_i, 0), (x_i + 1/n, 0), (x_i + a_i, 1).
Every triangle has base width 1/n on the line y = 0 and its apex on the line
y = 1. The objective is to choose x so that the AREA of the union of the n
triangles R_i is as small as possible. Here n = 64.

This baseline uses the classical Keich construction (valid for n a power of 2):
expand a_i = i/n in binary as a_i = sum_j eps_j 2^{-j} and set
    x_i = sum_{j=1}^{k} ((1 - j) / k) * eps_j * 2^{-j},   k = log2(n).

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (64,) with the base x-coordinates x_i.

kakeya_needle_3d8.docstring:
Three-dimensional discrete Kakeya needle problem with grid parameter N = 8.

We build N*N = 64 "generalized tubes" indexed by (i, j), i, j in {0, ..., N-1}.
Tube (i, j) has a base position (x, y) and, at height c in [0, 1], occupies the
axis-aligned square
    [x + c*i/N, x + 1/N + c*i/N] x [y + c*j/N, y + 1/N + c*j/N].
So the tube is a unit-height prism of square cross-section 1/N x 1/N that is
sheared so its top face is offset by (i/N, j/N): the (i, j) pair selects the
needle direction, and all N*N directions are covered. The task is to choose the
64 base positions so that the VOLUME of the union of all tubes is as SMALL as
possible (a Kakeya/Besicovitch-type set: needles in every direction, tiny measure).

Because the (i, j) grid is a full product and each square is a product of an
x-interval (a function of i) and a y-interval (a function of j), placing the base
x only as a function of i and the base y only as a function of j makes the union a
product of two 1-D unions. This baseline uses the Keich binary construction
(the 2-D Kakeya analogue, here for N = 2^k = 8) independently in x and y.

Returns:
    positions: np.ndarray of shape (64, 2). Row k = tube k in (i, j) raster order
        (i outer, j inner, i.e. numpy meshgrid indexing="ij" then flatten),
        column 0 = base x-coordinate, column 1 = base y-coordinate.

cylinders" problem). Each cylinder is described by its axis line: a point P on the

moving_sofa_2d.docstring:
The 2D moving-sofa problem: find the largest-area rigid shape that can be moved
through an L-shaped corridor of width 1 that makes a single 90-degree turn.

The shape is specified IMPLICITLY by a motion "path". Each path point is a triple
(x, y, angle_degrees) giving the position of the corridor's inner corner and the
corridor's rotation at one instant of the move. In the reference frame of the sofa
the corridor sweeps over the plane; the sofa is then the intersection of every
corridor placement along the path, so by construction it always clears the corridor.
The objective is to maximize the area of that intersection.

The evaluator prepends the start state (0, 0, 0) and appends the end state
(-2, 0, 90), then densifies the path to <=1-degree rotation steps, exactly as in the
AlphaEvolve "single turn" corridor notebook.

Returns:
    path: np.ndarray of shape (n, 3); each row is (x, y, angle_degrees) for the
        corridor's inner corner. Here n = 8. Endpoints are added by the evaluator.

moving_sofa_3d_path.docstring:
The 3D moving sofa problem: find the largest-volume rigid 3D shape that can
travel through an L-shaped 3D corridor of unit cross-section that has two
90-degree turns - one in the X-Y plane and one in the Y-Z plane (a 3D
generalisation of the classical 2D moving sofa problem).

The shape itself is recovered (in the evaluator) by sweeping a solid block
along a motion path and keeping every sub-volume that stays inside the
corridor for the whole path. The "solution" we evolve is therefore that
motion path: a sequence of rigid-body poses for the block.

A pose is a 6-tuple (x, y, z, yaw, pitch, roll), where (yaw, pitch, roll)
are extrinsic Euler angles in DEGREES (applied about the fixed z, y, x axes,
i.e. R = Rx(roll) @ Ry(pitch) @ Rz(yaw)) and (x, y, z) is a translation. To
place the block in a pose we first rotate it about the origin, then
translate it. The evaluator prepends a fixed start pose and appends a fixed
end pose, then densifies (smooths) the path before sweeping the block.

This baseline path is exactly the construction AlphaEvolve reported for this
problem in "Mathematical Discovery and Exploration at Scale" (2025), which
achieves a swept volume of about 1.81 at fine grid resolution.

Returns:
    path: np.ndarray of shape (99, 6), each row a pose
        (x, y, z, yaw_deg, pitch_deg, roll_deg).

no_5_on_a_sphere8.docstring:
The "no 5 on a sphere" problem. Select as many points as possible from the
n x n x n integer grid {0,...,n-1}^3 such that no five of the selected points
are co-spherical (lie on a common sphere, which also forbids five co-planar
points). Five points p_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i) are co-spherical iff the 5x5
determinant of rows [x_i, y_i, z_i, x_i^2 + y_i^2 + z_i^2, 1] vanishes.

Here n = 8. The objective is to MAXIMIZE the number of selected points.

Baseline construction (mirrors the notebook's randomized greedy search,
translated to pure numpy): run a fixed number of seeded random-order greedy
passes over the grid, adding a point whenever it keeps the set sphere-free,
and keep the largest set found. Deterministic via np.random.seed(0).

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (k, 3) of integer grid coordinates in
        [0, n-1], no five of which are co-spherical.

ovals_problem20.docstring:
The Ovals problem. For a fixed n, propose three real 1D arrays x, y and phi
(each of length n, viewed as samples at the equally spaced parameters
t_k = 2*pi*k/n, k = 0..n-1). Interpolating these periodically yields smooth
periodic functions f, g, h on [0, 2*pi]. Consider the planar curve
t -> (f(t), g(t)), reparametrized by arc-length s, with curvature kappa(s).
The objective is the Rayleigh quotient

    I(f, g, h) = integral_0^{2*pi} [ h'(s)^2 + (kappa(s) * h(s))^2 ] ds
                 / integral_0^{2*pi} h(s)^2 ds

which must be made AS SMALL AS POSSIBLE, subject to the curve being convex
(the signed curvature must stay strictly positive everywhere). Here n = 20.

Baseline construction: the unit circle with a constant weight, i.e.
x_k = cos(t_k), y_k = sin(t_k), phi_k = 1. For the circle the arc-length
curvature is identically 1 and h is constant, so I = 1 exactly.

Returns:
    (x, y, phi): a tuple of three np.ndarray each of shape (20,) giving the
        sampled values of the x-coordinate, y-coordinate and weight function.

cube, without any two unit cubes overlapping. Each cube is free to translate and

prime_number_theorem_partial_function.docstring:
Construct a partial function f from a subset of the positive integers to the reals
that maximizes a hidden number-theoretic objective related to the Prime Number Theorem.

The function f is scored by a fixed evaluator (see evaluator.py) that:
  * subtracts a constant from f(1) so that sum_k f(k)/k == 0,
  * requires the step function M(x) = sum_k f(k) * floor(x/k) to stay <= 1 for every
    real x in [1, 10*max_key] (otherwise the construction is infeasible), and
  * returns the objective a = -sum_k f(k) * log(k) / k (to be maximized; optimum 1.0).
The optimum is approached by the Mobius function mu(k), for which the classic identity
sum_{k<=x} mu(k) floor(x/k) = 1 holds and -sum mu(k) log(k)/k -> 1.

Representation:

rudin_problem10.docstring:
Rudin problem for polynomials on the 2-sphere. Find the real coefficients
(c_m) for m = -k..k of a real degree-k spherical harmonic

    f = sum_{m=-k}^{k} c_m Y_k^m

on the round unit sphere S^2 that MINIMIZE the norm ratio

    ||f||_{L^4(S^2)} / ||f||_{L^2(S^2)}

(norms taken with the standard surface measure dOmega of total mass 4*pi).
Here the degree is fixed to k = 10, so the returned vector has length
2*k + 1 = 21.

This baseline returns the all-ones coefficient vector (the same simple,
non-degenerate construction used in the upstream notebook's verification
cell); evolution should reshape these coefficients to flatten |f| and drive
the L^4/L^2 ratio down.

Returns:
    coeffs: np.ndarray of shape (21,) with the real coefficients
        c_m, ordered m = -10, -9, ..., 0, ..., 9, 10.

sendov_polynomial6.docstring:
Sendov's conjecture (probing the Sendov bound). For a complex polynomial f of degree n
with all zeros z_1,...,z_n in the closed unit disk, let w_1,...,w_{n-1} be its critical
points (the zeros of f'). The objective is to choose the n roots so as to maximize

    max_{1<=k<=n}  min_{1<=j<=n-1}  |z_k - w_j|

i.e. push some root as far as possible from every critical point. Sendov conjectured
this quantity never exceeds 1; the n-th roots of unity attain exactly 1. Here n = 6.

Returns:
    roots: np.ndarray of shape (6,), complex dtype, with every root inside the closed
        unit disk (|z_k| <= 1).

sidorenko_graphon.docstring:
Sidorenko's conjecture for the bipartite graph H = K_{5,5} minus a perfect
matching (10 vertices, 20 edges, 4-regular bipartite). A graphon is a symmetric
measurable function W: [0,1]^2 -> [0,1]; here it is represented as a step graphon,
i.e. a symmetric n x n matrix M with entries in [0,1] whose value on block (i,j)
equals M[i, j] (the unit square is split into n equal intervals).

Sidorenko's conjecture states that for every graphon W,
    t(H, W) >= t(K2, W)^|E(H)|,
i.e. the ratio  t(H, W) / t(K2, W)^|E(H)|  is at least 1. The goal is to make this
ratio as small as possible (a value strictly below 1 would be a counterexample).
The constant graphon W == 0.5 attains the ratio exactly 1 and is used as the seed.

Returns:
    M: np.ndarray of shape (8, 8), symmetric, with all entries in [0, 1] -
        the step-graphon matrix.

Place N = 12 points on the unit sphere S^2 so that they form a spherical 2-design:
the empirical first and second moments should match those of the uniform sphere.

which spreads 12 distinct points nearly uniformly over the sphere.

squares_in_square10.docstring:
Erdos "squares in a square" problem. Place n squares with pairwise disjoint
interiors inside the unit square [0,1]^2 so as to MAXIMIZE the sum of their
side lengths. Here n = 10.

Returns:
    centers: np.ndarray of shape (10, 2) with the (x, y) center of each square.
    sides:   np.ndarray of shape (10,) with the side length of each square.
The i-th axis-aligned square occupies
    [cx - s/2, cx + s/2] x [cy - s/2, cy + s/2].

Baseline construction: a simple deterministic grid packing. With
k = ceil(sqrt(n)) columns/rows and side = 1/k, the first n grid cells each
hold one square. This is feasible (squares only touch, never overlap, and
stay inside the unit square) but suboptimal.

Select as many points as possible from the 7x7 integer grid (x,y in {0,...,6})
such that no three selected points form an isosceles triangle. Three distinct
points are "isosceles" if at least two of their three pairwise squared distances
are equal. Maximize the number of selected points.

szemeredi_trotter_incidences.docstring:
Szemeredi-Trotter incidence maximization. Construct a set of n points and a set of
m lines in the plane (on the integer lattice) so as to maximize the number of
point-line incidences (pairs (p, l) with p lying on l). Here the instance is fixed
at n = 54 points and m = 27 lines.

Baseline: the classical Szemeredi-Trotter extremal grid construction with k = 3.
    Points:  {1,...,k} x {1,...,2*k^2}                          -> 2*k^3 = 54 points
    Lines :  y = a*x + b  for a in {1,...,k}, b in {1,...,k^2}  ->   k^3 = 27 lines
Each line y = a*x + b passes through exactly k of the grid points (one per column
x in {1,...,k}, since a*x + b stays within {1,...,2*k^2}), giving k^4 = 81 total
incidences. This matches the Szemeredi-Trotter bound n^(2/3) m^(2/3) up to a constant.

Lines are encoded in homogeneous form (A, B, C) meaning A*x + B*y + C = 0, so the
line y = a*x + b becomes (a, -1, b).

Returns:
    points: np.ndarray of shape (54, 2), integer (x, y) lattice coordinates.
    lines : np.ndarray of shape (27, 3), integer (A, B, C) with A*x + B*y + C = 0.

turan_hypergraph_tetrahedron.docstring:
Hypergraph Turan number of the tetrahedron. Construct a weighted, blow-up
3-uniform hypergraph pattern (vertex weights plus a multiset of size-3 edges)
that contains no copy of the tetrahedron K4^(3), so as to maximize the Turan
density lower bound C. The blow-up density of an edge multiset {a,b,c} over
the (sum-normalized) vertex weights w is:
    - 6 * w[a]*w[b]*w[c]            if a,b,c are all distinct,
    - 3 * w[dup]^2 * w[other]       if exactly two coordinates coincide,
    - w[a]^3                        if a == b == c,
and C is the sum of these contributions over all (distinct) edges.

Baseline: the classical 5/9 construction (Turan's conjectured optimum for
K4^(3)) on 3 weighted vertices.

Returns:
    weights: np.ndarray of shape (V,), non-negative vertex weights.
    edges: np.ndarray of shape (E, 3) of int vertex indices in [0, V-1];
        each row is a size-3 multiset (repeats allowed) of vertices.

name: Biology: protein multiple-alignment accuracy on BAliBASE reference alignments
description: Align the unaligned protein sequences of 26 BAliBASE reference-1 test cases, spanning very divergent and medium-divergence families. The evaluator checks that each alignment is a valid gapped version of the input sequences and scores the sum-of-pairs agreement with the structure-based reference alignment on its annotated core blocks.

sources.locator: Thompson, Plewniak and Poch (1999): comparison of multiple alignment programs on reference alignments; defines the sum-of-pairs and total-column scores on core blocks implemented here.
Thompson, Koehl, Ripp and Poch (2005): BAliBASE 3.0, the structure-based reference alignments and core-block annotations used as ground truth.
Katoh et al. (2002), MAFFT: an alignment method whose main goal is accurate and fast multiple sequence alignment, the problem this task scores.
BAliBASE download page; the archive BAliBASE_R1-5.tar.gz (reference sets RV11 and RV12 of this task) states no licence and is downloaded by the prepare script rather than redistributed.

requirements.datasets: Derived from the pinned BAliBASE 3.0 archive by python3 scripts/prepare_bio_physics.py (hashes in catalog/bio_physics-data-lock.json).

evaluation.benchmark: Biology: protein multiple-alignment accuracy on BAliBASE reference alignments
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: align(sequences) -> list of aligned rows, one per input sequence, all of the same length (at most 6 times the longest input sequence plus 10 columns), each row equal to its input sequence with '-' gap characters inserted (upper-case amino acids). sequences is a list of 4 to 10 unaligned protein sequences of a BAliBASE reference-1 test case. align is called once per test case in a sandboxed subprocess with a 240 s CPU budget for all 26 cases. Score (maximize): mean sum-of-pairs score over the cases, i.e. the fraction of residue pairs that the structure-based reference alignment places in the same core-block column and the candidate also aligns; the total-column score is reported alongside

limitations: Only 26 of the 82 reference-1 cases are used (at most 10 sequences and 300 reference columns each, and at least 43 core-block columns; ten further cases within the size limits, each with fewer than 40 core-block columns, are not used) so that a CPU-only aligner finishes within the budget; averages are therefore not comparable with published whole-benchmark numbers.

SP and TC are an independent implementation of the published definitions restricted to core blocks; it scores the reference alignments at exactly 1.0 but is not byte-compatible with the bundled bali_score program.
Reference alignments are themselves structure-based estimates of homology, and core blocks cover only part of each alignment.
The references are public, so search feedback can overfit this fixed subset; a candidate aligner should be checked on held-out families before any claim of improved accuracy.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value for this 26-case subset and local scorer. For context, the progressive-alignment seed reaches mean SP 0.640 (0.400 on the very divergent RV11 cases, 0.816 on RV12) and mean TC 0.480; published aligners report substantially higher SP on the full reference-1 sets, so there is room to improve.
