name: Finance: Daily volatility forecasting for US equity portfolios
description: Forecast the next day's return variance of the US stock market and 49 industry portfolios, updating the forecasts day by day from 2000 to 2025 after a training period ending in 1999. The evaluator reveals each day's returns only after the forecasts are made and scores the QLIKE loss against squared returns.

sources.locator: Hansen and Lunde (2005): out-of-sample comparison of many volatility models against GARCH(1,1) with several loss functions.
Patton (2011): loss functions, including QLIKE, that rank volatility forecasts consistently when the true variance is replaced by a noisy proxy such as the squared return.
Bollerslev (1986): the GARCH model, the classic benchmark for conditional variance forecasts.
Daily Fama/French factors (market = Mkt-RF + RF) and value-weighted 49 industry portfolio returns, CRSP 202509 files pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

requirements.datasets: Kenneth R. French Data Library daily factors and 49-industry returns (CRSP 202509 vintage) fetched by scripts/prepare_finance.py from pinned Internet Archive snapshots and verified by SHA-256; not redistributed.

evaluation.benchmark: Finance: Daily volatility forecasting for US equity portfolios
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: make_forecaster(training_returns, names) -> object with forecast() and update(returns). training_returns is a (7280, 50) float array of daily returns (decimal) from 1971-03-12 to 1999-12-31: column 0 is the CRSP value-weighted market (Mkt-RF + RF), columns 1-49 the value-weighted Fama-French industries; names lists the 50 series. The evaluator then walks through the 6,475 trading days 2000-01-03..2025-09-30: forecast() must return a (50,) array of next-day return variances in [1e-10, 1]; afterwards update(r) receives that day's (50,) returns. Score: mean QLIKE loss log(h) + r^2/h over all days and series (minimize); the RiskMetrics EWMA benchmark (lambda 0.94), the difference and a Diebold-Mariano statistic are reported. The candidate runs in a separate sandboxed process: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and the other installed packages are importable, while the evaluator's library, its data files, the network and subprocesses are not accessible; one thread and 3 GB of memory. It receives only the arguments described here, one call at a time: the arguments of a call are sent after the value of the previous call has been received. Arguments and return values travel as numbers, strings, lists, dicts with string keys and numeric numpy arrays, so a tuple arrives as a list

limitations: Squared daily returns are a noisy proxy for the daily variance; QLIKE ranks forecasts consistently with this proxy but the loss level is not a variance-accuracy measure, and intraday realized variances are not available here.
Forecasts are for close-to-close total returns (no mean adjustment); weekends, holidays and overnight effects are treated like any other trading day.

The evaluation period 2000-2025 is public. A candidate that reads the prepared files or memorizes returns can look ahead; the interface only passes returns up to the previous day. Treat scores as development scores.
One data vintage of CRSP value-weighted portfolio returns is used; the 50 series are strongly correlated, so they do not provide 50 independent comparisons.

The candidate runs in a sandboxed child process that never receives later data, realised outcomes or reference solutions, and no statement of the candidate is executed in the evaluator's process; outside macOS (kernel sandbox) deliberately hostile native code could bypass the file policy.

name: Few edges in 5-uniform hypergraphs without Property B (m(5))
description: construct() -> {'n': n, 'edges': [[v1, ..., v5], ...]}: distinct 5-element edges on vertices 0..n-1 with 5 <= n <= 26 and at most 200 edges. The hypergraph must have no proper 2-colouring (no colouring of the vertices leaves every edge with both colours), checked exactly by backtracking with unit propagation. Minimize the number of edges. A valid hypergraph with e edges certifies m(5) <= e; the best known construction has 51 edges and every 5-uniform hypergraph with at most 28 edges is 2-colourable.

The 51-edge construction was rebuilt locally on 17 vertices and verified non-2-colourable by exhaustive search. name: Shortest superpermutation on seven symbols
description: Write the shortest word over the symbols 1 to 7 that contains every one of the 5040 permutations of 1..7 as seven consecutive symbols. The shortest known word has 5905 symbols (A. Teodorescu, August 2026) and the best published lower bound is 5884.

sources.locator: Superpermutators mailing list, 18 August 2026: A. Teodorescu posts four length-5905 superpermutations for n = 7 (two distinct up to symmetry) found with G. Egan's PermutationChains.c and KernelFinder.c; A. Balint and S. Street confirm that they contain all 5040 permutations.
G. Egan's page: the previous record 5906 (Egan and Houston, 27 February 2019), its word, and the search programs.
R. Houston (2014), Tackling the minimal superpermutation problem.
Anonymous 4chan poster, R. Houston, J. Pantone and V. Vatter (2018): lower bound n! + (n-1)! + (n-2)! + n - 3, which is 5884 for n = 7.
OEIS A180632 (minimal superpermutation lengths): a(7) <= 5906 recorded in 2019.

requirements.datasets: None; the instance is defined by the parameters and no file is read at evaluation time.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct(n) -> a word over the symbols 1..n, given as a string of the digits 1..n or a list of integers; the evaluator passes this task's n. name: Minimal logarithmic energy of 100 points on the sphere
description: Place 100 points on the unit sphere to minimize the logarithmic energy, the sum over all pairs of log(1/distance), the energy in Smale's 7th problem. The lowest published energy, -1083.377140539, is the putative global minimum: it is not proven minimal, but random-restart local optimisation reproduces it within seconds, so the task measures whether an optimiser reaches it.

sources.locator: Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou (1994), Minimal discrete energy on the sphere: the minimal logarithmic and Riesz energy problems and numerical minima.
Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling (2014), supplement table 6.2 (s = 0): putatively minimal standardized pair energy v_0(100) = -0.21886406879576, i.e. E = -1083.377140539.

Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025), CC BY 4.0 dataset of local minima of the logarithmic energy; LocalMinima.zip, member 100.zip (39 minima for N = 100), whose lowest minimum reproduces the tabulated value to 2.9e-10.

requirements.datasets: None; the record value is embedded as a parameter and no file is read at evaluation time.

evaluation.benchmark: Minimal logarithmic energy of 100 points on the sphere
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3) of nonzero vectors; each is normalised to the unit sphere. Score: the logarithmic energy sum_{i<j} log(1 / |x_i - x_j|) (natural logarithm, chordal distances, pair terms summed with math.fsum); minimize. Points closer than 1e-9, a wrong shape or non-finite values make the candidate invalid.

limitations: The record is the lowest published value we could check: the tables of Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling (2014), compiled from Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou (1995) and Calef (2009), and the 2025 landscape survey of Amore, Figueroa and Ramos. R. Womersley's published point sets could not be accessed when the task was prepared, so a lower value in sources we could not read cannot be excluded.
Points are normalised to the unit sphere before scoring, so only directions matter; the record coordinates are public, so scores measure the returned construction, not the search that produced it.
Candidate Python runs inside the evaluator process and is trusted research code; the evaluator recomputes the score from the returned array but does not sandbox the program.

The reference is easy to reach: L-BFGS on the normalised coordinates from random starting points ties it within the 1e-9 margin in about a second (55 of 129 random starts in 35 s on one core for N = 100), no start went below it, and the 39 local minima published by Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025) contain no lower value. The headroom of the task is therefore the gap between the seed and this value; a score below it by more than the margin would be a new record and is not expected.

state_of_the_art.statement: The lowest published logarithmic energy we found for 100 points on the unit sphere is E = -1083.377140539 (standardized pair energy v_0 = -0.21886406879576 in the data tables of Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling 2014, compiled from Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou 1995 and Calef 2009). The lowest of the 39 local minima published by Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025) attains it to 2.9e-10. No minimizer is proven for this N; rigorous results exist only for a few small N such as N = 6 and N = 12.

state_of_the_art.statement: The lowest published logarithmic energy we found for 150 points on the unit sphere is E = -2364.632242592 (standardized pair energy v_0 = -0.21160020067937 in the data tables of Nerattini, Brauchart and Kiessling 2014, compiled from Rakhmanov, Saff and Zhou 1995 and Calef 2009). The lowest of the 6094 local minima published by Amore, Figueroa and Ramos (2025) attains it to 9.0e-11. No minimizer is proven for this N; rigorous results exist only for a few small N such as N = 6 and N = 12.

name: Smallest Mahler measure above one in degree at most 12 (Lehmer's problem)
description: construct() -> integer coefficients [c_0, ..., c_d] (constant term first) with 1 <= d <= 12, |c_i| <= 3 and c_d != 0. Polynomials equal to +-x^k times a product of cyclotomic polynomials (measure exactly one) are rejected by exact polynomial division. The score is the Mahler measure |c_d| * prod max(1, |z|) over all complex roots z (Aberth iteration, reported to 10 decimals). Minimize; the optimum is Lehmer's number 1.1762808183. Among integer polynomials of degree at most 12 the least measure above one is Lehmer's number, so the task recovers Lehmer's polynomial (up to sign, reversal and cyclotomic factors).

sources.locator: Michael J. Mossinghoff, Georges Rhin and Qiang Wu, Minimal Mahler Measures (2008). Crossref records inspected for Lehmer (Ann. of Math. 1933), Smyth (Bull. LMS 1971) and Mossinghoff, Rhin and Wu (Experimental Math. 2008). Lehmer's polynomial x^10 + x^9 - x^7 - x^6 - x^5 - x^4 - x^3 + x + 1 has measure 1.17628081826; Mossinghoff, Rhin and Wu determined the minimal measure of noncyclotomic irreducible polynomials of every even degree up to 54, none below Lehmer's number, and Smyth proved that nonreciprocal polynomials (which include every noncyclotomic irreducible polynomial of odd degree) have measure at least 1.3247. Measures multiply over factors, so no integer polynomial of degree at most 12 has measure in (1, 1.17628). Among integer polynomials of degree at most 12 the least measure above one is Lehmer's number, so the task recovers Lehmer's polynomial (up to sign, reversal and cyclotomic factors).

execution.interface: construct(instance) -> array of shape (n, 3): Cartesian coordinates of n atoms in reduced units. instance = {'potential': 'dzugutov', 'n': atoms, 'A', 'B', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'm'}; called once for each n in (38, 45, 50, 55, 57, 60); all calls together within 300 s (enforced) and should use at most 4 threads (not enforced by the evaluator). The evaluator recomputes E = sum_{i<j} V(r_ij) with V(r) = A(r^-m - B)exp(c/(r - a)) [r < a] + B exp(d/(r - b)) [r < b], A = 5.82, B = 1.28, a = 1.87, b = 1.94, c = 1.10, d = 0.27, m = 16; atoms must be at least 0.5 apart. execution.interface: fit_predict(train_inputs, train_targets, test_inputs, info) -> list of len(test_inputs) floats. Inputs are ordered crystal structures {'lattice': 3x3 lattice vectors as rows (Angstrom), 'species': element symbols, 'frac_coords': fractional coordinates per site}. Called once per official Matbench v0.1 fold (five calls, KFold(5, shuffle, random_state=18012019)), each in a fresh process that receives that fold's training inputs with targets and its held-out inputs without targets; info = {'task', 'input_type', 'target', 'unit', 'fold', 'n_train', 'n_test'}. Runs in a separate process that receives only these arguments (no test values), with at most 4 threads (OMP/MKL/OpenBLAS set to 4), no network, no subprocesses and no read access to the repository or prepared data; numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and RDKit are importable (pandas and torch only where the environment provides them; they are not requirements of the task); wall-clock limit 170 s per fold. Score: mean over the five folds of the held-out mean absolute error in target units (minimize), the Matbench leaderboard metric

limitations: All targets are public in the Matbench files and every sample is a test sample of one fold; candidates or settings tuned on these folds overfit, so treat scores as development scores.

Leaderboard entries were trained without this task's limits (170 s and at most 4 CPU threads per fold, CPU only), so leaderboard values are reference points rather than targets attainable under the same budget.
Targets are OptB88vdW DFT values, not measurements, with a heavy tail (up to 1604 meV/atom) that dominates fold MAEs; 636 samples.

Candidates run in a separate process that never receives held-out values, but the process isolation is an audit-hook policy for honest program search, not a security boundary (ctypes stays available for scientific libraries); run adversarial evaluations in a container.

execution.interface: fit_predict(train_inputs, train_targets, test_inputs, info) -> list of len(test_inputs) labels, each 0 or 1 (1 = metal). Inputs are compositions {'formula': str, 'composition': {element: amount}}; training targets are 0/1. Called once per official Matbench v0.1 fold (five calls), each in a fresh process that receives that fold's training inputs with labels and its held-out inputs without labels; info = {'task', 'input_type', 'target', 'unit', 'fold', 'n_train', 'n_test'}. Runs in a separate process that receives only these arguments (no test values), with at most 4 threads (OMP/MKL/OpenBLAS set to 4), no network, no subprocesses and no read access to the repository or prepared data; numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and RDKit are importable (pandas and torch only where the environment provides them; they are not requirements of the task); wall-clock limit 170 s per fold. Score: mean over the five folds of the balanced accuracy of the labels, the "mean balanced accuracy" column of the Matbench leaderboard (for 0/1 labels it equals the binary ROC AUC) (maximize); accuracy and F1 are reported

limitations: All labels are public in the Matbench file and every sample is a test sample of one fold; candidates or settings tuned on these folds overfit, so treat scores as development scores.
Leaderboard entries were trained without this task's limits (170 s and at most 4 CPU threads per fold), so leaderboard values are reference points.

Only 0/1 labels are accepted, so the score is the balanced accuracy; ROC AUC from probabilities, which Matbench also accepts, would not be comparable with the leaderboard entries that submitted labels. Labels are deduplicated by composition, so polymorphs share one label.

Candidates run in a separate process that never receives held-out values, but the process isolation is an audit-hook policy for honest program search, not a security boundary (ctypes stays available for scientific libraries); run adversarial evaluations in a container.

name: Sutton-Chen transition-metal cluster global minima
description: Find the lowest-energy structures of 38- to 80-atom clusters of the Sutton-Chen many-body metal potential with the silver, nickel and gold parameter sets (six instances). Energies are recomputed exactly and compared with the putative global minima of Doye and Wales.

sources.locator: Doye and Wales (1998): Sutton-Chen 12-6, 9-6 and 10-8 clusters, table of putative global minima for N <= 80 (arXiv cond-mat/9711038).
Sutton and Chen (1990): the long-range Finnis-Sinclair potential and its (n, m, c) parameters.
Lopez-Castro, Ortiz-Chi and Merino (2024): GrowPAL search over Sutton-Chen clusters with 5-80 atoms; reports new lower minima for 12-6 N = 68 and 10-8 N = 58 (not used here).
LaTeX source of the global-minimum table (four decimals).

requirements.datasets: None; reference energies are published values embedded in the evaluator.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct(instance) -> array of shape (n, 3): Cartesian coordinates of n atoms in reduced units (lattice constant 1). instance = {'potential': 'sutton_chen', 'kind': '12-6' | '9-6' | '10-8', 'n': atoms, 'n_exp', 'm_exp', 'c'}; called once for each of six instances (kind, n) = (12-6, 38), (12-6, 75), (9-6, 59), (9-6, 80), (10-8, 55), (10-8, 79); all calls together within 300 s (enforced) and should use at most 4 threads (not enforced by the evaluator). The evaluator recomputes E = sum_i [1/2 sum_{j!=i} r_ij^-n_exp - c sqrt(sum_{j!=i} r_ij^-m_exp)] over all pairs (no cutoff) with (n_exp, m_exp, c) = (12, 6, 144.41), (9, 6, 39.432), (10, 8, 34.408); atoms must be at least 0.35 apart. Score: mean over instances of 100*(E - E_pub)/|E_pub| against the putative global minima tabulated by Doye and Wales (1998) (minimize; 0 matches all six, negative is lower). chem_clusters.relax(positions, 'sutton_chen', kind) and chem_clusters.sutton_chen_energy_gradient(positions, kind) may be called

limitations: References are the 1998 putative minima (four decimals); the Cambridge Cluster Database listed the same six energies on 2026-11-24, and its coordinate files score them with this evaluator within 5e-5. Lopez-Castro et al. (2024) report database-level minima for all sizes from 5 to 80 except three (lower energies for 12-6 N = 68 and 10-8 N = 58, not reproduced for 10-8 N = 60); those three are excluded.
Putative minima are public, so remembered structures score well without search; the energy is computed without a cutoff, as in the source, and differs from implementations that truncate the sums.
The score averages relative energy excesses over six instances within a shared 300 s budget.

name: Odd covering systems with moduli dividing 51975 (fewest uncovered residues)
description: construct() -> classes [[m, r], ...] with distinct moduli m > 1 dividing 51975 = 3^3 * 5^2 * 7 * 11 (hence odd) and 0 <= r < m. The score is the number of residues modulo 51975 covered by no class (exact). Minimize. The score 0 (a covering system with distinct odd moduli) is impossible for this modulus by the necessary condition of Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel (1986). Every divisor of 51975 above 1 is available once. The minimum is positive: an odd covering with distinct moduli needs prod (p-1)/(p-2) - sum 1/(p-2) > 2 over the primes p dividing the least common multiple (Berger, Felzenbaum and Fraenkel), and for 3, 5, 7, 11 the left side is 86/45. The score measures how close systems with this modulus come to a covering; it cannot decide the odd covering problem. No minimum is documented.

name: Contact numbers of 32 unit pennies on the triangular lattice
description: construct() -> exactly 32 distinct integer pairs [a, b] with |a|, |b| <= 64 denoting lattice points a + b*omega, omega = exp(i*pi/3), which are at mutual distance at least one. name: Physics: broadband antireflection coating design
description: Design a stack of at most twenty low- and high-index layers (1.38 and 2.35) on glass that minimizes the mean reflectance between 400 and 800 nm at normal incidence, with at most 1000 nm of total coating. The evaluator checks the constraints and computes the reflectance spectrum exactly with the thin-film characteristic-matrix method.

sources.locator: Dobrowolski, Tikhonravov, Trubetskov, Sullivan and Verly (1996), Optimal single-band normal-incidence antireflection coatings: how the lowest attainable average reflectance depends on bandwidth, index contrast and total optical thickness.
Tikhonravov, Trubetskov and DeBell (1996), Application of the needle optimization technique to the design of optical coatings: the standard numerical method for this design problem.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; the materials and specification are defined in the evaluator.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: design(problem) -> (materials, thicknesses): a list of 'L'/'H' labels and a list of physical thicknesses in nm, layers ordered from the air side to the substrate. problem gives ambient_index 1.0, substrate_index 1.52, materials {'L': 1.38, 'H': 2.35} (lossless, non-dispersive), band_nm [400, 800], max_layers 20, max_total_nm 1000 and max_layer_nm 400; every thickness must lie in [0, max_layer_nm] and the sum must not exceed max_total_nm. design runs in a sandboxed subprocess with a 60 s CPU budget. Score (minimize): mean normal-incidence reflectance in percent over 401 equally spaced wavelengths in the band, computed exactly with the characteristic-matrix method (bare glass: 4.26 %)

limitations: Layers are lossless and non-dispersive with fixed indices, and only normal incidence is scored; real coatings need dispersion data, absorption, oblique incidence and tolerance to thickness errors.

The specification (two materials, 400-800 nm, 20 layers, 1000 nm) is a local choice in the spirit of Dobrowolski et al. (1996); no published optimum exists for it, so scores compare designs under this model only.
The mean is taken over 401 equally spaced wavelengths, so a design could in principle exploit the sampling between grid points; the reported maximum reflectance helps to spot that.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value for this exact specification. For context, bare glass reflects 4.26 %, the single quarter-wave seed gives 1.58 %, and a multistart local optimization of alternating 14-layer stacks run during task construction reached 0.084 %.

name: Physics: exact quantum circuit synthesis within published CNOT budgets
description: Compile seven fixed two- and three-qubit unitaries (CNOT, iSWAP, SWAP, the Toffoli gate and three generic unitaries) into single-qubit rotations and CNOT gates without exceeding the CNOT counts known to suffice for each. The evaluator rebuilds every circuit's unitary exactly and scores the mean phase-insensitive distance to the targets.

sources.locator: Shende, Bullock and Markov (2006), Synthesis of quantum-logic circuits: quantum Shannon decomposition with twenty CNOTs for any three-qubit unitary and the lower bound of fourteen.
Vatan and Williams (2004), Optimal quantum circuits for general two-qubit gates: three CNOTs suffice for every two-qubit unitary and SWAP needs three.
Shende and Markov (2009), On the CNOT-cost of TOFFOLI gates: six CNOTs are necessary and sufficient for the Toffoli gate.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; the targets and the Hamiltonian are defined in the evaluator.

evaluation.benchmark: Physics: exact quantum circuit synthesis within published CNOT budgets
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: synthesize(problem) -> list of gates. problem has keys name, qubits (2 or 3), cnot_budget and the target unitary as real and imaginary (nested lists of 2**qubits rows). A gate is ['u3', qubit, theta, phi, lam] for the standard single-qubit rotation or ['cx', control, target] for a CNOT; qubit 0 is the most significant bit of the basis index. At most cnot_budget CNOTs and 400 gates per circuit. synthesize is called once per target in a sandboxed subprocess with a 150 s CPU budget for all seven targets. Score (minimize): mean over the targets of the phase-insensitive distance 1 - |tr(target^dagger U)| / 2**qubits, where the evaluator rebuilds U from the gate list; 0 means exact synthesis of every target within its budget

limitations: Each CNOT budget is known to be achievable, so the optimum score (0) is known; the task measures whether a synthesis procedure finds exact circuits numerically within a fixed CPU budget, not whether it beats a published bound.
The gate set is limited to U3 rotations and CNOTs on all-to-all connectivity; hardware topology, gate errors and compilation time are not modelled.
The two-qubit and three-qubit generic targets are three fixed matrices defined in the evaluator, so the score does not average over the unitary group.
Distances below about 1e-12 are at floating-point resolution and count as exact.

state_of_the_art.statement: Exact synthesis within every budget is known to be possible: three CNOTs for any two-qubit unitary (two for iSWAP, one for CNOT), six for the Toffoli gate and twenty for any three-qubit unitary, so the minimum score 0 is attainable.

science_relevance.importance_rationale: CNOT count is the dominant cost of running a quantum circuit on hardware; the optimal counts for two- and three-qubit unitaries are classical results of quantum circuit synthesis, and numerically finding circuits that attain them is what compilers must do.

name: Physics: product-formula design for Heisenberg-chain time evolution
description: Choose the coefficients of a twelve-stage product formula that approximates the time evolution of a six-site Heisenberg chain split into even and odd bonds. The evaluator builds every factor and the exact propagator and scores the mean spectral-norm error at three evolution times.

sources.locator: Childs, Su, Tran, Wiebe and Zhu (2021), Theory of Trotter error with commutator scaling: commutator bounds on the spectral-norm error of product formulas for quantum simulation.
Suzuki (1990), Fractal decomposition of exponential operators: the higher-order product formulas built from symmetric splittings.
Blanes and Moan (2002), Practical symplectic partitioned Runge-Kutta and Runge-Kutta-Nystrom methods: optimized splitting coefficients for a fixed number of stages.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; the targets and the Hamiltonian are defined in the evaluator.

evaluation.benchmark: Physics: product-formula design for Heisenberg-chain time evolution
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: coefficients(stages) -> (a, b), two lists of 12 finite numbers in [-50, 50] with sum(a) = sum(b) = 1 (consistency). The evaluator forms the product formula U(t) = S_12 ... S_2 S_1 with S_k = exp(-i b_k t B) exp(-i a_k t A): stage 1 acts first, and within a stage the A factor acts before the B factor. With sites numbered 0..5 and Pauli matrices X, Y, Z, the Hamiltonian of the six-site open XXZ chain (anisotropy 0.8, field 0.3) is H = sum_{j=0..4} (X_j X_{j+1} + Y_j Y_{j+1} + 0.8 Z_j Z_{j+1}) + 0.3 sum_{j=0..5} Z_j = A + B, where A holds the bonds (0,1), (2,3), (4,5) and the field on sites 0, 2, 4, and B holds the bonds (1,2), (3,4) and the field on sites 1, 3, 5. Score (minimize): mean over t = 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 of the spectral norm ||U(t) - exp(-i t (A + B))||. coefficients runs in a sandboxed subprocess with a 60 s CPU budget

limitations: The error is measured on one six-site chain and three evolution times; coefficients tuned here need not be optimal for other Hamiltonians, system sizes or step sizes.
The fixed stage count fixes the cost per step only in this two-group splitting; circuit depth and hardware costs of a quantum implementation are not modelled.
Errors are computed on the full 64-dimensional Hilbert space by dense linear algebra; this is exact for this size but does not scale to larger chains.
No published value exists for this exact chain, stage count and set of times.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value for this chain and protocol. For context, the evaluator gives 0.046 for repeated Strang splitting (the seed) and 0.31 for Suzuki's fourth-order formula with five Strang substeps, which loses at the largest time because its large coefficients amplify the error at big steps.

sources.title: Theory of Trotter error with commutator scaling

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Approximate the time evolution of a quantum spin chain by a product of exponentials of simpler terms with as little error as possible for a given number of factors.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Product formulas are the standard way to simulate quantum dynamics on digital quantum computers, and the error of a given formula at a given step size determines the circuit depth needed for a target accuracy; designing better coefficients is an active line of work in both quantum simulation and geometric numerical integration.

name: Physics: photonic-crystal unit cell with a large higher-order TM band gap
description: Design a symmetric 32x32-pixel unit cell of air and dielectric (epsilon 12) for a two-dimensional square-lattice photonic crystal that opens the largest gap between the fourth and fifth TM bands. The evaluator solves the band structure with an exact-coefficient plane-wave method over the irreducible Brillouin zone and scores the gap-midgap ratio.

sources.locator: Cox and Dobson (1999), Maximizing band gaps in two-dimensional photonic crystals: the gap-maximization problem for TM and TE polarizations on a square lattice.
Men, Nguyen, Freund, Parrilo and Peraire (2010): band-gap optimization of symmetric square-lattice cells on a 1/32 grid with air and a dielectric, including higher TM gaps such as the fourth.
Sigmund and Hougaard (2008), Geometric properties of optimal photonic crystals: topology-optimized band-gap structures.
MPB Python tutorial: the rod crystal (epsilon 12, radius 0.2a) has TM gaps of 38.95 % (bands 1-2) and 3.84 % (bands 4-5); used to check the local solver.

requirements.datasets: None downloaded; the materials, lattice and solver are defined in the evaluator.

evaluation.benchmark: Physics: photonic-crystal unit cell with a large higher-order TM band gap
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: design(problem) -> 32 x 32 nested list of 0/1 pixels of one square unit cell (1 = dielectric with epsilon 12, 0 = air), invariant under the square symmetry group about the cell centre (cell == cell[::-1] row-wise and column-wise and cell == its transpose). problem gives pixels 32, eps_low 1, eps_high 12, lower_band 4 and polarization TM. design runs in a sandboxed subprocess with a 120 s CPU budget. The evaluator computes TM bands with a 289-plane-wave Galerkin method using the exact Fourier coefficients of the pixel map, on 30 wave vectors covering the boundary and interior of the irreducible Brillouin zone. Score (maximize): gap-midgap ratio 2 (min omega_5 - max omega_4) / (min omega_5 + max omega_4) between TM bands 4 and 5; negative when the bands overlap

limitations: The evaluator is a 289-plane-wave Galerkin solver on a 32-pixel grid: designs are scored under this discretization, which is converged to about 0.1 percentage points on test structures but is not a full-wave simulation of a fabricated device.
Band extrema are searched on 30 wave vectors of the irreducible zone (boundary plus interior samples), standard for symmetric cells but able to miss extrema between samples.
Only one polarization and one gap (TM bands 4-5) are optimized; complete band gaps and fabrication constraints such as minimum feature size are not part of the score.
Published optimized gaps (Men et al. 2010) use an eigenvalue-based gap ratio and a finite-element discretization, so they are not directly comparable with this score.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value under this exact discretization and gap measure. For context, the textbook rod crystal (the seed) gives 0.0431 here, against 3.84 % in the MPB tutorial for the same nominal structure (the difference comes from the pixelated circle and from the tutorial's grid resolution), and a 150-second greedy pixel-flip search run during task construction reached 0.311.

name: Physics: two-dimensional spin-glass ground states on fixed instances
description: Find ground states of nine Edwards-Anderson spin glasses on 10x10, 15x15 and 20x20 periodic square lattices with Gaussian couplings. The evaluator recomputes the cut weight of every returned spin configuration and compares it with the exact optimum computed for these instances by branch-and-cut.

sources.locator: Liers, Juenger, Reinelt and Rinaldi (2004) compute exact ground states of Ising spin glasses by branch-and-cut and introduce these toroidal grid instances with Gaussian couplings.

Barahona (1982) shows that the spin-glass ground-state problem is polynomially solvable on two-dimensional lattices without a field and NP-hard in three dimensions and in two dimensions with a field. The instances of this task are periodic in both directions (toroidal, not planar); for the torus, polynomial algorithms are known for integer couplings bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size (Galluccio, Loebl and Vondrak, Math. Program. 90 (2001) 273-290, doi:10.1007/PL00011425).

Biq Mac library: the t2g torus instances (ising_all.tar.gz) and their optimal cut values in Table 10 of biqmaclib.pdf; no licence stated, so the archive is downloaded by the user and not redistributed here.

requirements.datasets: Derived from the pinned Biq Mac archive by python3 scripts/prepare_bio_physics.py (hashes in catalog/bio_physics-data-lock.json).

evaluation.benchmark: Physics: two-dimensional spin-glass ground states on fixed instances
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: ground_state(instance) -> list of instance['nodes'] spins, each -1 or +1. instance has keys name, nodes, side, dimension and edges (list of [i, j, weight] with integer weights and 0-based node indices) of a 2-dimensional periodic grid of side 10, 15 and 20 with Gaussian couplings. ground_state is called once per instance in a sandboxed subprocess with a 180 s CPU budget for all nine instances together. Score (maximize): mean over the instances of cut_weight / published_optimal_cut, where the evaluator recomputes the cut weight from the edge list; 1.0 means reaching the exact optimum everywhere. The spin-glass energy of the couplings J = -weight is sum(weight) - 2 * cut_weight, so a larger cut is a lower energy

limitations: The reference values are the optimal cut weights published with the library, obtained by branch-and-cut with no time limit; the task gives a candidate a few minutes of CPU for nine instances, so matching them is hard and the score is budget-dependent.

Planar two-dimensional lattices without a field are polynomially solvable by matching (Barahona 1982), but these instances are toroidal: for graphs on the torus, polynomial algorithms are known when the integer couplings are bounded by a polynomial in the lattice size (Pfaffian enumeration; Galluccio, Loebl and Vondrak 2001, who credit Barahona 1982 for toroidal square lattices). The couplings here are integers up to about 3.8e5, so that method is pseudo-polynomial for these instances. A transfer-matrix dynamic programme over rows solves the three 10x10 instances exactly in seconds and confirms their published optima; it does not scale to 15x15 and 20x20 within the budget, where the task is a test of heuristics.
Only these nine fixed instances are scored: a better score is a better heuristic on them, not a statement about the Edwards-Anderson model in general.
Couplings are the integer-scaled Gaussian weights of the published instances; the evaluator reports the corresponding spin-glass energy but scores the cut weight.

state_of_the_art.statement: The optimal cut weights of these nine instances are known exactly (6049461, 5757868, 6509837 for 10x10; 15051133, 15763716, 15269399 for 15x15; 24838942, 29290570, 28349398 for 20x20), so a score of 1.0 is attainable and cannot be exceeded.

Couplings are the integer-scaled Gaussian weights of the published instances; the evaluator reports the corresponding energy but scores the cut weight.
Ground-state degeneracy is not examined: the task only measures how close the recomputed cut weight comes to the published optimum.

NP-hardness is a worst-case statement and these instances have at most 343 spins: simulated annealing with a few hundred replicas reaches the published optimum of eight of the nine instances within seconds each (the ninth to within 3e-4), so a score close to 1.0 is attainable inside the budget and the headroom of the task is the gap between the seed (0.885) and 1.0.

execution.interface: angles(n, coupling, field, layers) -> finite real array (layers,n) in radians. H=-coupling*sum Z_i Z_(i+1)-field*sum X_i, open chain, qubit i is bit i. name: Software engineering: history-based test prioritisation in continuous integration (ABB IOF/ROL)
description: Order the test cases of each of the 320 continuous-integration cycles of ABB's IOF/ROL system so that failing tests run early, using only the verdicts of earlier cycles. Each cycle's verdicts are revealed after its order is committed; the score is the mean APFD over cycles with both failing and passing tests.

sources.locator: Spieker, Gotlieb, Marijan and Mossige (ISSTA 2017): reinforcement learning for test prioritisation and selection in CI; introduces the ABB Paint Control and IOF/ROL data.
Pinned atcs-data commit (MIT licence): paintcontrol.csv and iofrol.csv with cycle, test, duration and verdict columns.
Elbaum, Rothermel and Penix (FSE 2014): history-based test prioritisation and selection in continuous integration at Google.
Rothermel, Untch, Chu and Harrold (TSE 2001): test case prioritisation and the APFD metric.

requirements.datasets: ABB IOF/ROL CI history from HelgeS/atcs-data at commit 85bae8b6 (MIT), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: history-based test prioritisation in continuous integration (ABB IOF/ROL)
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: prioritize(cycle, history) -> list of int. cycle = {'cycle': int, 'tests': [{'id': int, 'duration': int}, ...]} lists the test cases of one continuous-integration cycle, sorted by id (durations are the data set's approximate run times). history lists every earlier cycle in order as {'cycle': int, 'tests': [{'id', 'duration', 'failed': bool}, ...]}. Return a permutation of the cycle's test ids, the test to run first first. A cycle's verdicts are revealed, by appending it to history, only after its order has been committed. Score: mean APFD over the cycles that contain both failing and passing tests, maximised; APFD = 1 - (sum of the 1-based positions of the m failing tests) / (n m) + 1 / (2 n) for a cycle of n tests, so a random order scores 0.5 in expectation. prioritize() is called once per cycle, all cycles in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU in total, 2 GB); module-level state persists between calls. It should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks); an invalid order makes the evaluation invalid.

limitations: The verdicts are historical: the order cannot change which tests fail, and every test of a cycle is assumed to run.

Plain APFD with each failing test counted as one fault; the source paper reports NAPFD under a time budget, so its numbers are not directly comparable. Durations are given to the candidate but not used by the metric.
Repeated executions of a test within one cycle are merged (failed if any execution failed); the data set's LastRun and LastResults columns and its row order are not passed on.
Ordering failing tests first gives 0.815 on this data; a last-verdict heuristic (the seed) gives 0.585, and 99 of the 320 cycles contain a single test.
The verdicts are public; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

state_of_the_art.statement: Published results on this data use NAPFD under a time budget or other aggregations, so no directly comparable value is embedded; the best possible score for this metric (failing tests first) is reported in the evaluator details.

name: Software engineering: pairwise covering array for the Apache configuration model
description: Build a smallest pairwise covering array for the 172-option Apache web-server model of Cohen et al., avoiding its forbidden option combinations. Every feasible pair of option settings must appear in some test configuration; fewer configurations is better.

sources.locator: Cohen, Dwyer and Shi (TSE 2008): constrained interaction testing of highly configurable systems; introduces the SPIN, GCC, Apache and Bugzilla constraint models and a SAT-checked greedy construction.
Jia, Cohen, Harman and Petke (ICSE 2015): hyperheuristic search for constrained covering arrays; publishes the benchmark archive used here.
ICSE15_HHSA_Benchmarks.zip (CC BY 4.0): CASA-format model and constraint files; levels are numbered from 1.
Supplementary table of the FastCA repository: HHSA and CASA sizes (2-way and 3-way, 5-hour cutoff) on the same HHSA-format instance files.

requirements.datasets: One CASA model from the ICSE 2015 CIT benchmark archive (Zenodo 581657, CC BY 4.0), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: pairwise covering array for the Apache configuration model
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: generate(model) -> list of rows. model = {'name': str, 'strength': t, 'values': [v_0, ..., v_{k-1}], 'forbidden': [[[p, level], ...], ...]}: parameter p takes a level in 0..v_p-1 and each forbidden entry lists parameter-level pairs that must not all occur in one row. Return a list of rows, each a list of k Python ints. Every row must avoid all forbidden combinations, and the rows together must contain every combination of levels of t distinct parameters that occurs in at least one valid configuration (the evaluator decides feasibility exactly). Score: number of rows, minimised; an array that misses a feasible combination or contains a forbidden one is invalid. generate() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; CPU limit 60 s for pairwise and 120 s for 3-way tasks, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Published sizes on these exact files: HHSA 30 rows and CASA 32 rows (FastCA repository supplementary table, minimum over runs with a 5-hour cutoff).
The array size is the only objective; generation time is bounded by the sandbox CPU limit and is not scored, whereas the published solvers ran for 1000 s to 5 h in C++.
Feasible combinations are decided by an exact search at preparation time and cross-checked with Z3 in the tests; a Z3 disagreement would change the required set.
The models are public; a candidate could embed a precomputed array. Scores are comparable with published sizes only for arrays generated within the contract.

state_of_the_art.statement: HHSA reports a 30-row pairwise array on this model (FastCA repository supplementary table). No valid array can have fewer rows: the 6-level and 5-level options have 30 feasible level pairs, which must occur in distinct rows (counting bound recomputed here). The published array itself was not re-checked here. The value therefore equals the counting lower bound: it is the optimum, so this instance cannot show a new state of the art.

name: Software engineering: optimal register coalescing on the 22 largest challenge graphs
description: Colour the 22 interference graphs with 3,000 to 28,640 nodes from the Appel-George Optimal Coalescing Challenge with 6 registers so that as much move (affinity) weight as possible joins nodes of the same colour. The score is the mean share of affinity weight left uncoalesced; lower is better.

sources.locator: Appel and George, Optimal Coalescing Challenge (2000): 474 interference graphs with affinities, problem and solution format, checker and published solution sets.
Appel and George (PLDI 2001): optimal spilling by integer programming followed by coalescing; source of the challenge graphs.
George and Appel (TOPLAS 1996): iterated register coalescing, the heuristic behind the published greedy solution set.
Grund and Hack (CC 2007): cutting-plane ILP for optimal coalescing; their solutions of all 474 challenge instances are on the challenge page.
Park and Moon (TOPLAS 2004): optimistic register coalescing, the basis of the published optimistic solution set.

requirements.datasets: Optimal Coalescing Challenge graphs and the published Grund-Hack, iterated-coalescing and optimistic solution sets (no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URLs and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: optimal register coalescing on the 22 largest challenge graphs
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: coalesce(problem) -> list of int. problem = {'name': str, 'nodes': N, 'registers': K (6 in every instance), 'interference': [[i, j], ...], 'affinities': [[i, j, w], ...]} with nodes numbered 0..N-1: nodes 0..K-1 are machine registers and node i < K must get colour i; every other node interferes with fewer than K nodes, so a legal colouring always exists; affinities are move-related pairs with positive integer weights. Return N Python ints in 0..K-1 such that no interference pair shares a colour. Cost of an instance: total weight of the affinity pairs whose two nodes get different colours. Score: mean over the task's instances of cost divided by the instance's total affinity weight (the share of move weight not coalesced), minimised; 0 means every move is coalesced. An illegal colouring of any instance makes the evaluation invalid. coalesce() is called once per instance, all instances in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 3 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Best-known costs are the published Grund-Hack ILP solutions; CPLEX proved 19 of the 22 optimal, while instances 139, 304 and 387 stopped after five minutes. Blazy and Robillard (LCTES 2009) report optimal solutions for these three, which were not checked here.
The score averages per-instance shares of uncoalesced affinity weight; the challenge itself evaluates instances separately, so totals in the literature are not the same number.
All graphs come from one compiler (SML/NJ) with six registers after optimal spilling; methods tuned on them may not transfer to other register files or allocators.
The instances are public; a candidate could embed precomputed colourings, which the contract excludes.
The candidate gets 120 s of CPU time in total in a Python sandbox; published solvers had no comparable limit.

state_of_the_art.statement: Mean uncoalesced share of the Grund-Hack ILP solutions (19 of 22 proven optimal), recomputed here. The published iterated-register-coalescing and optimistic-coalescing solution sets score 0.0268 and 0.0155.

name: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
description: Rank the code blocks of a faulty module by suspiciousness using only its program spectrum: for each block, how many failing and passing tests execute it. The 532 faults are first-order mutants of textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions; the score is the mean EXAM (rank of the faulty block divided by the number of blocks).

sources.locator: Jones and Harrold (ASE 2005): the Tarantula fault-localisation technique and its evaluation by the share of code examined (the seed).
Abreu, Zoeteweij and van Gemund (TAIC PART 2007): accuracy of spectrum-based fault localisation with block hit spectra; Ochiai coefficient.
Wong, Debroy, Gao and Li (IEEE Trans. Reliability 2014): the DStar formula.
Yoo (SSBSE 2012): evolving risk-evaluation formulas with genetic programming, the program-search setting of this task.
Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017): results on artificial faults do not carry over to real faults; the main caveat of this task.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence); spectra derived by scripts/prepare_software.py with the evaluator's mutants and test pools.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: localize(spectrum) -> list of float. spectrum = {'subject': 'textwrap', 'urllib.parse' or 'fractions', 'blocks': n, 'failed': F, 'passed': P, 'ef': [n ints], 'ep': [n ints]} describes one faulty version of the module: F of its pool tests fail (their outcome differs from the correct module's) and P pass, and ef[b] (ep[b]) is the number of failing (passing) tests that execute block b, where blocks are the evaluator's block probes (function entries, branch outcomes, loop bodies and exits, handlers) in a random order that is drawn anew for every fault and every evaluation, so an index does not denote the same block in different faults or evaluations; the faults are presented in a random order as well. Return n finite numbers, a suspiciousness per block (higher means more likely faulty). Score: mean EXAM over the 532 faults, i.e. the faulty block's rank (ties count as their average rank) divided by n, minimised. localize() is called once per fault, all faults in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Faults are artificial first-order mutants, one per version; Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017) found that rankings of fault-localisation techniques on artificial faults do not predict their rankings on real faults.

Spectra are block hit counts from this evaluator's probes and a seeded 240-call test pool per module, not statement coverage of a project's own test suite; the faulty block is the statement-level block containing the mutated statement (faults on one-line compound statements are left out), so EXAM values are not comparable with published ones.
Undetected mutants and mutants that break the import are excluded; textwrap contributes 110 faults, urllib.parse 183 and fractions 239.

Reference values computed here: Tarantula (the seed) 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM; ranking each faulty block first among blocks with an identical spectrum would give 0.0087, a bound for formulas of the counts that no single formula need reach.

Blocks and faults are shown in a random order that changes with every evaluation, so neither a position nor the number of the call carries information; the score of a formula of the counts does not depend on the order. The faults are public, however: a spectrum identifies its fault, and a search can still overfit this fault set.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for these faults. Computed with this evaluator: Tarantula 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM.

name: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's html.parser
description: Generate at most 1,000 input strings that drive html.parser.HTMLParser with _markupbase (CPython 3.12.14) through as many code blocks as possible. The score is the number of distinct instrumented blocks (function entries, branch outcomes, loop exits, handlers) that the inputs reach.

sources.locator: Bohme, Pham and Roychoudhury (CCS 2016): coverage-based greybox fuzzing, where reaching new coverage guides input generation.
Godefroid, Kiezun and Levin (PLDI 2008): grammar-based fuzzing of parsers to reach code beyond the lexer.
Klees, Ruef, Cooper, Wei and Hicks (CCS 2018): how fuzzers are evaluated, including coverage as a measure.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the pure-Python target modules and the test inputs used as references.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: coverage-guided fuzzing of CPython's html.parser
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: fuzz(target) -> list of str. target = {'subject': str, 'entry': str (how one input is executed), 'files': {path: source} (the subject's CPython 3.12.14 files as the evaluator loads them), 'instrumented': [paths whose coverage counts], 'max_inputs': 1000, 'max_chars': 2000}. Return at most max_inputs strings of at most max_chars characters. The evaluator imports the files under a private package name, inserts a numbered probe at the start of every block inside the functions of the instrumented files (function entry; if and else branches, including an empty else; loop bodies and normal loop exits; try bodies, else and finally blocks; exception handlers; with bodies; match cases; both branches of conditional expressions), runs the entry on every input (exceptions are expected and ignored; an input is cut off after 1,000,000 steps, where a step is a function entry or a loop iteration inside a function of the instrumented files, so the cut does not depend on the machine, or after 5 s of CPU time, a safety net for time spent in C code; probes reached before the cut count) and counts the distinct probes reached. Entries: tomllib -> tomllib.loads(text); re -> re._compiler.compile(text, 0), i.e. regular-expression parsing and compilation; html.parser -> for convert_charrefs in (True, False): HTMLParser(convert_charrefs).feed(text) then close(); plistlib -> plistlib.loads(text.encode('latin-1')), so each character U+0000-U+00FF is one byte and the XML or binary format is detected from the bytes (characters above U+00FF only raise the encoding error). Score: number of distinct probes reached, maximised; replaying all inputs may take at most 120 s of CPU time, otherwise the evaluation is invalid. fuzz() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU, 2 GB) and may load and run the given files itself, for example to trace coverage; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Coverage is a proxy: no faults are seeded and crashes are not scored, while fuzzing research also measures bugs found (Klees et al. 2018).
Block probes are this evaluator's own instrumentation of the pinned sources (no coverage.py or compiler edges), so counts are not comparable with other coverage tools; some probes are unreachable.
The corpus is bounded by size (1,000 strings of at most 2,000 characters) and generation by 60 s of CPU time instead of the hours-long wall-clock budgets of fuzzing benchmarks.
Reference computed here: the 525 distinct string constants of CPython's test_htmlparser.py reach 172 of the 372 probes; the random-string seed reaches fewer.
The target is pure Python executed by CPython; results say nothing about memory-safety bugs in C code.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this instrumentation. As a reference, the 525 distinct string constants of CPython's test_htmlparser.py reach 172 of the 372 probes (computed with this evaluator).

name: Software engineering: log parsing (event template identification) on the 16 Loghub-2k data sets
description: Group the messages of 16 system logs (2,000 lines each, from HDFS, Hadoop, Spark, Linux, OpenSSH and others) by the log statement that produced them, given only the message texts. The score is the mean grouping accuracy against the corrected ground-truth events.

execution.interface: parse(dataset) -> list. dataset = {'name': one of Android, Apache, BGL, HDFS, HPC, Hadoop, HealthApp, Linux, Mac, OpenSSH, OpenStack, Proxifier, Spark, Thunderbird, Windows, Zookeeper, 'messages': [2000 str]} gives the message contents of 2,000 log lines of one system in their original order (header fields such as time, level and component already removed). Return one group label (int or str) per message; messages with equal labels are claimed to come from the same log statement (event template). Grouping accuracy of a data set: the share of messages whose group contains exactly the messages of their ground-truth event, no more and no fewer. Score: mean grouping accuracy over the 16 data sets, maximised. parse() is called once per data set, all data sets in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); per-data-set settings are allowed, as in the published benchmarks; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Grouping accuracy is the classic metric; later work also reports parsing accuracy of the template strings and template-level F1 (Jiang et al., ISSTA 2024), which are not scored here.
Each data set has only 2,000 messages, and newer, larger annotations (Loghub-2.0) show lower accuracies for the same parsers; results here say little about scale.

The candidate gets message contents with the headers already removed by the benchmark's log formats, so header parsing is not part of the task; per-data-set settings, as in the published benchmarks, are allowed.

Reference values computed with this evaluator: logparser's Drain with its benchmark settings scores 0.8605 mean grouping accuracy on the corrected labels (0.8654 on the original labels, as published); the digit-masking seed scores 0.7937.
The logs and their labels are public; embedding labels is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically. The Loghub licence permits research or academic use with attribution only.

state_of_the_art.statement: No directly comparable published value exists for the corrected labels. As a reference computed with this evaluator, logparser's Drain (He et al. 2017) with its published benchmark settings scores 0.8605 mean grouping accuracy on these labels; on the original Loghub-2k labels it scores 0.8654, reproducing the published table exactly. Language-model-based parsers report higher accuracies but are outside this CPU contract.

name: Software engineering: loop-invariant inference for the Code2Inv programs
description: Infer a loop invariant for each of the 124 valid Code2Inv C programs so that Z3 proves initiation, consecution and the post-condition. The procedure may query a verifier that returns counterexamples (50 queries per program); the score is the fraction of programs with a proven invariant.

sources.locator: Si, Dai, Raghothaman, Naik and Song (NeurIPS 2018): Code2Inv, learning loop invariants with a verifier in the loop; introduces the 133-program benchmark.
Pinned Code2Inv benchmark directory: C programs (C_instances/c) and SMT-LIB verification conditions (C_instances/c_smt2); no licence stated.
Ryan, Wong, Yao, Gu and Jana (ICLR 2020): CLN2INV; removes 9 invalid programs and solves all 124 others (LoopInvGen 104, Code2Inv 90), one hour per problem.
Garg, Loding, Madhusudan and Neider (CAV 2014): ICE learning, invariant inference from a teacher's implication and counterexamples.
Flanagan and Leino (FME 2001): Houdini, the template-based invariant pruning used by the seed.

requirements.datasets: Code2Inv C programs and verification conditions (PL-ML/code2inv at commit 336a7063, no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URL and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: synthesize(problem, oracle) -> str. problem = {'name': str, 'c_source': str (declarations, pre-condition assignments, one while loop and a post-condition assert), 'variables': [names of the integer program variables], 'definitions': str (the Code2Inv SMT-LIB definitions of pre-f, trans-f and post-f over the variables, their primed next-state copies and SSA auxiliaries), 'max_queries': 50}. Return a loop invariant as one SMT-LIB Boolean term over the variables using integer literals (write negative numbers as (- n)), true, false and the operators and, or, not, =>, ite, =, <, <=, >, >=, +, -, * (at most one non-constant factor), div and mod (positive literal divisor), i.e. linear integer arithmetic. It is correct when Z3 proves initiation (pre-f implies it), consecution (it and trans-f imply it for the primed variables) and safety (it implies post-f), each within a fixed resource limit. oracle(invariant) performs the same check and returns {'valid': bool, 'failed': 'initiation', 'consecution', 'safety', 'syntax' or a budget message, 'state': a counterexample assignment of the variables or None, 'next': the successor assignment for consecution failures or None, 'queries_left': int, 'error': parse error if any}; each problem allows 50 queries and all queries share a fixed Z3 resource budget. Score: fraction of the 124 valid programs whose returned invariant is correct, maximised; a returned str that does not parse counts as not proven, a non-str answer makes the evaluation invalid. synthesize() is called once per program, all programs in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses, so Z3 is not available there; 180 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Of the 133 programs, bounded model checking here finds 9 whose post-condition can fail (26, 27, 31, 32, 61, 62, 72, 75, 106), the count reported by Ryan et al. (2020); those 9 are excluded, so scores use 124 programs.
Five of the 124 post-conditions hold at every loop exit, so the invariant 'true' already proves them; many others need only simple bounds.

Correctness follows the benchmark's own SMT-LIB verification conditions, checked by Z3 with a fixed resource limit; the C programs themselves are not executed, so an error in an encoding would carry over.

Invariants are restricted to linear integer arithmetic and the candidate has 50 verifier queries per program and 180 s of CPU in total, while published tools had one hour per program and unbounded solver calls (LoopInvGen averaged about 3,600 calls); published counts are therefore not directly comparable.
The programs are public and solved invariants circulate; embedding them is outside the contract but cannot be checked automatically.
Results depend on the Z3 version only where a check reaches the resource limit; this run used z3-solver 5.1.0.

state_of_the_art.statement: CLN2INV proves all 124 valid programs (LoopInvGen 104, Code2Inv 90) with one hour per program and unbounded solver calls (Ryan et al. 2020, Table 1); their invariants were not re-checked with this evaluator. The score is the fraction of programs proven, so 1.0 is its maximum: the optimum is attained and this instance cannot show a new state of the art.

name: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's fractions
description: Generate at most 30 test calls for fractions.Fraction (parsing, arithmetic, rounding, formatting) that distinguish as many of its 453 first-order mutants as possible from the original module. A mutant is killed when some test's result or exception type differs; the score is the fraction killed.

sources.locator: Fraser and Zeller (TSE 2012): generating unit tests and oracles that kill mutants.
DeMillo and Offutt (TSE 1991): constraint-based generation of test data that kills mutants.
Lukasczyk, Kroiss and Fraser (EMSE 2023): automated unit test generation for Python (Pynguin), assessed by coverage and mutation score.
Papadakis, Jia, Harman and Le Traon (ICSE 2015): trivial compiler equivalence for removing equivalent mutants.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): the mutated modules.

requirements.datasets: CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: mutation-adequate test generation for CPython's fractions
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: generate_tests(subject) -> list of tests. subject = {'subject': str, 'files': {path: source} (CPython 3.12.14), 'target': path of the mutated module, 'api': {call: [argument kinds]}, 'mutants': [{'unit', 'operator', 'line', 'start', 'end', 'replacement'}, ...], 'max_tests': 30}. A test is {'call': name, 'args': [values]}. Argument kinds: 'str' (at most 500 characters), 'int' (|n| <= 10000), 'opt_int' (such an int or None), 'bool', 'float' (finite, |x| <= 1e6), 'fraction' (a str of at most 30 characters for Fraction(), with an exponent of at most two digits), 'spec' (a format spec of at most 12 characters without runs of four digits), 'number' (a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 1000 or a float), 'numbers' (a list of at most 40 values, each a 'fraction' str, an int with |n| <= 10000 or a float with |x| <= 1e6), 'pairs' (at most 20 [str, str] pairs of at most 100 characters each), {'options': {keyword: kind}} (keyword arguments), {'strings': n} (exactly n strings), {'choice': [allowed values]}. Calls: textwrap: wrap/fill/shorten(text, width, options) -> textwrap.<call>(text, width, **options), dedent(text), indent(text, prefix); urllib.parse: each call is the function of that name with the arguments in order (urlparse/urlsplit(url, scheme, allow_fragments), urljoin(base, url, allow_fragments), parse_qs/parse_qsl(qs, keep_blank_values, strict_parsing, max_num_fields, separator), quote/quote_plus(string, safe)), urlunparse/urlunsplit get the strings as a tuple, urlencode(pairs, doseq, safe) passes the pairs as tuples; fractions: parse(s) -> Fraction(s), make(n, d) -> Fraction(n, d), from_float(x), binary(a, op, b) applies the operator (or divmod, max) to a and b with str operands converted by Fraction, limit_denominator(s, m), round(s, ndigits) (round(Fraction(s)) when ndigits is None), format(s, spec) -> format(Fraction(s), spec), method(s, name) -> getattr(Fraction(s), name)(); statistics (str values become Fraction): summary(name, data) -> statistics.<name>(data), median_grouped(data, interval), quantiles(data, n, method), weighted(name, data, weights) -> fmean or harmonic_mean with weights, spread_given_center(name, data, c) -> variance/pvariance/stdev/pstdev(data, c), bivariate(name, x, y) -> covariance, correlation (linear or ranked) or linear_regression (proportional or not), normal(mu, sigma, method, x) -> NormalDist(mu, sigma).method(x) (quantiles(int(x)) for 1 <= x <= 1000, overlap(NormalDist(x, 1.0))), from_samples(data). A mutant is the target file with lines start..end replaced by 'replacement'; it is killed when some test's outcome differs from the original module's outcome, where the outcome is a hash of the repr of the result (generators consumed, at most 10,001 items) or the type name of the raised exception. A call is cut off, with the outcome 'timeout', when it exceeds 50,000 steps or its CPU-time limit. A step is a function entry or a loop iteration inside a function of the given files, so the count does not depend on the machine (the largest call the argument bounds allow needs about 10,000 steps). The CPU-time limit is 0.2 s on the original module and 0.2 s plus ten times the original's own CPU time on a mutant; it only matters for calls that spend long inside C code or whose iterations grow ever more expensive. Tests that time out on the original are ignored. Score: killed mutants / all mutants, maximised (equivalent mutants make 1.0 unreachable); the whole mutation analysis may take at most 240 s of CPU time, otherwise the evaluation is invalid. generate_tests() runs in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 60 s CPU, 2 GB) and may load the files and mutants itself; it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks). Invalid tests make the evaluation invalid.

limitations: Mutants come from this evaluator's operator set (MutPy- and mutmut-style replacements inside function bodies); scores are not comparable with other mutation tools.
Non-compiling, duplicate and trivially compiler-equivalent mutants are removed, but other equivalent mutants remain, so 1.0 is unreachable and the number of killable mutants is unknown.
Oracles are regression oracles: a test kills a mutant when the hash of the result's repr or the exception type differs from the original's, which also counts differences a specification might allow.

Reference computed with this evaluator (Linux x86-64, CPython 3.12): the seed's generate_tests with max_tests = 2000, i.e. 2,000 random calls, kills 239 of the 453 mutants (52.8%); the 30-test budget is this dataset's choice.
The candidate sees the mutants and may run them, so the task measures test generation and selection against known mutants, not generalisation to unseen faults.

name: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
description: Write a synthesiser that, from a few input-output examples and a grammar, returns a string-manipulation program (phone numbers, names, initials, university addresses) that also reproduces held-out examples of the same task. The score is the fraction of 27 SyGuS-Comp tasks solved.

sources.locator: Gulwani (POPL 2011): FlashFill, synthesising string transformations in spreadsheets from input-output examples.
Alur et al. (FMCAD 2013): syntax-guided synthesis, the problem format (grammar plus specification) of these tasks.
Alur, Radhakrishna and Udupa (TACAS 2017): EUSolver, enumerative synthesis with divide and conquer, evaluated on SyGuS PBE string tasks.
Padhi, Millstein, Nori and Sharma (CAV 2019): overfitting in synthesis, programs that fit the examples but not the intended function.
Pinned SyGuS benchmarks (no licence stated): the base and '-long' files of the 27 tasks.

requirements.datasets: SyGuS-Org/benchmarks PBE_SLIA_Track/from_2018 at commit 13c8deb6 (no licence stated; fetched from the pinned URL and not redistributed), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: programming by example for string transformations (SyGuS-Comp PBE strings)
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: synthesize(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'function': str, 'params': [[name, sort], ...], 'sort': 'String', 'start': nonterminal, 'grammar': [[nonterminal, sort, [productions]], ...], 'examples': [[[argument strings], output string], ...]} is a SyGuS PBE string problem: productions are parameter names, literals (string literals as {'str': value}, integers, true, false), other nonterminals or operator lists such as ['str.substr', 'ntString', 'ntInt', 'ntInt']. Return one SMT-LIB term (an S-expression string; string literals in double quotes with "" for a quote, negative numbers as -1 or (- 1)) that the grammar derives from 'start'. Operations follow SMT-LIB 2.6 string semantics (str.++, str.len, str.at, str.substr, str.indexof, str.replace, str.to.int, int.to.str, str.prefixof, str.suffixof, str.contains, +, -, =, ite, with the edge cases of the standard, e.g. out-of-range str.at and str.substr give "" and str.to.int of a non-numeral gives -1). A task is solved when the term reproduces the given examples and the held-out examples of the benchmark's '-long' variant. Score: fraction of the 27 tasks solved, maximised; a term that does not parse or leaves the grammar counts as unsolved, a non-str answer makes the evaluation invalid. synthesize() is called once per task, all tasks in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).

limitations: Only 27 tasks, from a few families (11 phone-number tasks, 4 name-combination tasks, 6 university-address tasks and 6 others), so scores move in steps of 1/27 and families are correlated.

Correctness is judged on examples: the given ones plus 8 to 94 held-out examples of the '-long' variant per task (3 to 94 distinct ones, because the long files repeat examples; bikes has 3); a program that agrees on all of them but differs elsewhere counts as solved.

SyGuS-Comp scored consistency with the given examples and solving time, not generalisation, so published solved counts are not comparable; the benchmark repository notes that errors and duplicates may exist.

name: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
description: Write a general repair procedure that receives a buggy QuixBugs Python program with a few visible tests and returns a patch of at most two statements. A patch counts only when it also passes held-out QuixBugs tests and generated tests whose expected outputs come from the reference fix.

sources.locator: Lin, Koppel, Chen and Solar-Lezama (SPLASH Companion 2017): the QuixBugs benchmark of 40 programs with one-line bugs in Python and Java.
Pinned QuixBugs commit (MIT licence): python_programs, correct_python_programs (used only at preparation time) and json_testcases.
Le Goues, Nguyen, Forrest and Weimer (TSE 2012): GenProg, test-suite-based generate-and-validate repair.
Smith, Barr, Le Goues and Brun (ESEC/FSE 2015): patches that pass the repair tests but fail held-out tests (overfitting).
Ye, Martinez, Durieux and Monperrus (JSS 2021): repair tools on QuixBugs; plausible patches checked for overfitting with generated tests.

requirements.datasets: QuixBugs at commit 4257f44b (MIT), prepared by scripts/prepare_software.py; the reference fixes are used only to derive held-out tests and are not stored.

evaluation.benchmark: Software engineering: test-based repair of the QuixBugs Python programs
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: repair(task) -> str. task = {'name': str, 'entry': str, 'source': str, 'tests': [{'input': [arguments], 'expected': value, 'tolerance': float (only for sqrt)}, ...], 'max_statement_edits': 2}: 'source' is a buggy QuixBugs Python program defining the function 'entry'; 'tests' are its visible tests, at least one of which fails. Return the patched program as a str of at most 20000 characters that differs from 'source' in at most 2 statements (replaced, inserted or deleted statements of the parsed program; formatting and comments do not count). A test passes when entry(*input) returns the expected value after JSON normalisation (generators are consumed into lists, tuples become lists), or a number within 'tolerance' of it, within the test's step limit. A step is one function entry or one loop iteration of the program, counted by the evaluator, so the limit does not depend on the speed of the machine: 2,000,000 steps per test, and 25,000,000 for the test levenshtein('rosettacode', 'raisethysword'), on which the reference fix makes 10,308,990 calls (on every other test the reference fixes need at most 761,717 steps). A CPU-time limit of 10 s plus 2 microseconds per allowed step remains as a safety net for programs whose steps are individually slow. Score: fraction of the 31 programs whose patch passes its visible tests, its remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated held-out tests whose expected values come from the reference fix (higher is better); a patch passing only some of them counts as overfitting, not repaired. repair() runs once per program in a sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 4 s CPU, 1 GB) and may execute the given program and tests itself; it should be deterministic. The procedure must be general: remembered program-specific fixes are outside the contract. A repair() call that raises, exceeds its limits or returns something other than a str of at most 20000 characters makes the whole evaluation invalid.

limitations: Uses the 31 Python programs with JSON tests; the nine graph programs are excluded, so results reported on all 40 programs are not comparable, nor are results of tools that call language models.

Correctness is decided by tests: the visible tests, the remaining QuixBugs tests and 10 to 40 generated inputs per program checked against the reference fix. A semantically different but test-equivalent patch counts as a repair, and a wrong patch that agrees on all these inputs would also count; there is no manual patch review.
Generated inputs respect the documented preconditions and avoid inputs whose correct output is not unique; inputs on which the reference fix itself loops (some wrap cases) are excluded.
The programs and their fixes are public, so a candidate could embed remembered fixes; the contract excludes this but it cannot be checked automatically.
Each repair() call gets 4 s of CPU time in a Python sandbox, far less than the hours given to repair tools in the literature.

The suite's evaluator template imports the candidate module in the evaluator process before scoring; every scored call runs in the sandbox, which cannot read the held-out data, but deliberately hostile import-time code could. Untrusted evaluations should run in a container without the prepared files.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published result uses this 31-program subset with these held-out tests. Ye et al. (2021) report repair tools on all 40 Java QuixBugs programs, and language-model studies report counts on all 40 Python programs under other correctness criteria.
